113\title[The low-dimensional structures formed by tricategories]{The low-dimensional structures\\formed by tricategories}
114\author{Richard Garner}
115\address{Department of Mathematics, Uppsala University, Box 480, S-751 06 Uppsala,
116Sweden}\email{richard@math.uu.se}
117\author{Nick Gurski}
118\address{Department of Mathematics, Yale University, 10 Hillhouse Avenue,
119PO Box 208283, New Haven, CT 06520-8283, USA}
120\email{michaeln.gurski@yale.edu}

124\maketitle
125\begin{abstract}
126We form tricategories and the homomorphisms between them into a bicategory,
127whose $2$-cells are certain degenerate tritransformations. We then enrich this
128bicategory into an example of a three-dimensional structure called a
129\emph{locally cubical bicategory}, this being a bicategory enriched in the
130monoidal 2-category of pseudo double categories. Finally, we show that every
131sufficiently well-behaved locally cubical bicategory gives rise to a
132tricategory, and thereby deduce the existence of a tricategory of
133tricategories.
134\end{abstract}
135\section{Introduction}
136A major impetus behind many developments in 2-dimensional category theory has
137been the observation that, just as the fundamental concepts of set theory are
138categorical in nature, so the fundamental concepts of category theory are
1392-categorical in nature. In other words, if one wishes to study categories ``in
140the small''~--~as mathematical entities in their own right rather than as
141universes of discourse~--~then a profitable way of doing this is by studying
142the 2-categorical properties of $\cat{Cat}$, the 2-category of all
143categories.\footnote{Here, and elsewhere, we will adopt a common-sense attitude
144to set-theoretic issues, assuming a sufficient supply of Grothendieck universes
145and leaving it to the reader to qualify entities with suitable constraints on
146their size.}
147Once one moves from the study of categories to the study of (possibly weak)
148$n$-categories, it is very natural to generalise the above maxim, and to assert
149that \emph{the fundamental concepts of $n$-category theory are
150$(n+1)$-categorical in nature.} This is a profitable thing to do: for example,
151consider the coherence theorem for bicategories \cite{MLP}, which in its
152simplest form states that
153\[\text{\emph{Every bicategory is biequivalent to a 2-category.}}\]
154\textit{A priori}, this is merely a statement about individual bicategories;
155but we may also read it as a statement about the tricategory of bicategories
156$\cat{Bicat}$, since ``biequivalent'' may be read as ``internally biequivalent
157in the tricategory $\cat{Bicat}$.''\footnote{In practice, one would tend to use
158the local definition of biequivalence, wherein $\B$ is biequivalent to $\B'$ if
159there exists a homomorphism $F \colon \B \to \B'$ which is biessentially
160surjective on objects and locally an equivalence of categories; but as long as
161we assume the axiom of choice, the difference between the two definitions is
162merely one of presentation.}\ \ Thus another way of stating the above would be
163to say that the 2-categories are biequivalence-dense in $\cat{Bicat}$.
164This maxim permeates almost all research in higher-dimensional category theory,
165and so we draw attention to it here, not in order to point out where we might use
166it, but rather where we might \emph{not} use it. For instance, consider once
167again the coherence theorem for bicategories. We may restate it slightly more
168tightly as:
169\begin{gather*}\text{\emph{Every bicategory is biequivalent to a
1702-category}}\\\text{\emph{via an identity-on-objects
171biequivalence.}}\end{gather*} The restriction to identity-on-objects
172biequivalences affords us an interesting simplification, since, as pointed out
173in \cite{LP}, we can express such a biequivalence as a mere \emph{equivalence}
174in a suitable 2-category, which we denote by $\cat{Bicat}_2$. The 0-cells of
175$\cat{Bicat}_2$ are the bicategories; the 1-cells are the homomorphisms between
176them; and the 2-cells are the \emph{icons} of~\cite{Lackicons}. These are
177degenerate oplax natural transformations whose every $1$-cell component is an
178identity: we will meet them in more detail in Section~\ref{bicat-tricat} below.
179With the help of the 2-category $\cat{Bicat}_2$, the coherence theorem for
180bicategories can be made into a 2-categorical, rather than a tricategorical,
181statement: namely, that the 2-categories are equivalence-dense in
182$\cat{Bicat}_2$ (cf. Theorem 5.4 of \cite{LP}). This is a somewhat tighter
183result; moreover, the 2-category $\cat{Bicat}_2$ is much simpler to work with
184than the tricategory $\cat{Bicat}$.
185Thus we should revise our general maxim, and acknowledge that \emph{some} of the fundamental concepts of $n$-category theory may be expressible using fewer than $(n+1)$ dimensions.
186Consequently,
187when we study $n$-categories, it may be useful to form them not only into an $(n+1)$-category, but also into suitable lower-dimensional structures.
188It is
189the purpose of this paper to do this in the case $n=3$. We construct both a
190bicategory of tricategories $\cat{Tricat}_2$ and a tricategory of tricategories
191$\cat{Tricat}_3$: where in both cases, the 2-cells are suitably scaled-up
192analogues of the bicategorical icons mentioned above.
193In \cite{Lackicons}, Lack gives a number of motivations for studying the
1942-category $\cat{Bicat}_{2}$ of bicategories, lax functors, and icons. Many of
195these motivations have obvious analogues one dimension higher. For instance,
196the coherence theorem for tricategories can be restated as
197\[\text{\emph{Every tricategory is internally biequivalent to a $\cat{Gray}$-category
198in the tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_{3}$.}}\] On the other hand, coherence for
199tricategories internal to the \textit{bicategory} $\cat{Tricat}_{2}$ is an open
200question. The structures $\cat{Tricat}_{2}$ and $\cat{Tricat}_{3}$ also
201provide avenues for studying the simplicial nerves of tricategories, thus
202allowing comparisons with work of Street \cite{streetomega} to be pursued in
203dimension three. Moreover, it is shown in~\cite{Lackicons} that the
204$2$-category of monoidal categories embeds nicely in $\cat{Bicat}_{2}$; and
205similarly, we show that the tricategory of monoidal bicategories~--~as
206constructed in \cite{cheng-gurski}~--~embeds nicely in $\cat{Tricat}_{3}$.
207An outline of the paper is as follows. In Section~\ref{bicat-tricat}, we
208construct a bicategory of tricategories, $\cat{Tricat}_{2}$. The construction
209is straightforward and computational. The 2-cells of this bicategory we call
210\textit{ico-icons}: they can be seen as doubly degenerate oplax
211tritransformations whose $0$- and $1$-cell components are identities. More
212explicitly, they exist only between trihomomorphisms which agree on $0$- and
213$1$-cells, and are given by a collection of (not necessarily invertible)
214$3$-cell components together with coherence data and axioms.
215In Section~\ref{Sec:towards}, we describe a tricategory of tricategories,
216$\cat{Tricat}_3$. The first candidate we consider for its $2$-cells are the
217\emph{oplax icons}, which are singly degenerate oplax tritransformations: they
218exist only between trihomomorphisms which agree on $0$-cells, and are given by
219a collection of (not necessarily invertible) $2$- and $3$-cell components
220together with coherence data and axioms. These generalise the $2$-cells of
221$\cat{Tricat}_2$, since every ico-icon is an oplax icon: indeed, the ico-icons
222are precisely the \emph{i}dentity \emph{c}omponents \emph{o}plax icons.
223However, oplax icons turn out to be too lax to compose properly: the same phenomenon which occurs if one tries to replace the weak transformations in the tricategory $\cat{Bicat}$ with oplax transformations.
224Thus
225instead we take the $2$-cells of $\cat{Tricat}_3$ to be the smaller class of \emph{pseudo-icons}: these being oplax icons whose $3$-dimensional data is invertible.
226Although we describe the tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$ in
227Section~\ref{Sec:towards}, we do not complete its construction. One reason is
228that we want to avoid giving unenlightening tricategorical coherence
229computations as far as possible, to which end, we would like to reuse the work
230we did in Section~\ref{bicat-tricat}; and though intuitively this is not a
231problem, technically it is rather troublesome. A second reason is that we wish
232to explain an unusual discrepancy, namely that the bicategory $\cat{Tricat}_2$
233carries some information which the tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$ cannot, in that
234an ico-icon ($2$-cell of $\cat{Tricat}_2$) cannot be viewed as a pseudo-icon
235($2$-cell of $\cat{Tricat}_3$) unless it is \emph{invertible}.
236In Sections~\ref{Sec:locallydouble}--\ref{Sec:fromltt} we describe a general
237mechanism which allows us to clear up both of the above issues. This begins in
238Section~\ref{Sec:locallydouble} with the introduction of a new kind of
239three-dimensional categorical structure which we call a \emph{locally cubical
240bicategory}. Like a tricategory, it has $0$-, $1$-, $2$-, and $3$-cells; but
241the $2$-cells come in two different kinds, vertical and horizontal, whilst the
242$3$-cells are cubical in nature. Moreover, the coherence axioms that are to be
243satisfied are of a bicategorical, rather than a tricategorical kind, and so the
244resultant structure is computationally more tractable than a tricategory. As a
245first application of this theory, we are able to show quite easily that the
246totality of bicategories (and more generally the totality of \emph{pseudo
247double categories} in the sense of~\cite{GP1}) form a locally cubical
248bicategory.
249%
250%We may summarise this by saying that a locally cubical bicategory is a
251%\emph{bicategory enriched in the monoidal bicategory of pseudo double
252%categories}.
253Section~\ref{Sec:local} then describes a locally cubical bicategory of
254tricategories which we denote by $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$. The construction is
255once again straightforward and computational, and reuses the work done in
256Section~\ref{bicat-tricat}. The objects and $1$-cells of $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$
257are just tricategories and trihomomorphisms; the vertical $2$-cells are the
258ico-icons from $\cat{Tricat}_2$; the horizontal $2$-cells are the pseudo-icons
259from $\cat{Tricat}_3$; whilst the $3$-cells are ``cubical icon modifications''.
260In particular, $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$ is a rich enough structure to encode all
261the information from both $\cat{Tricat}_2$ and $\cat{Tricat}_3$. This resolves
262the second of the issues mentioned above.
263In order to resolve the first issue, we appeal to a general theory which allows
264us to construct tricategories out of sufficiently well-behaved locally cubical
265bicategories: more precisely, those with the property that every invertible
266vertical $2$-cell gives rise to a horizontal $2$-cell. This general theory is
267described in detail in Section~\ref{Sec:fromltt}; whilst in
268Section~\ref{tritri}, we are able to apply it to the locally cubical bicategory
269$\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$, thereby deducing the existence of the tricategory of
270tricategories $\cat{Tricat}_3$. Additionally, we identify the tricategory of
271monoidal bicategories inside of $\cat{Tricat}_{3}$.

330\textbf{Notation.}\ \ \ We follow \cite{bicats} and \cite{review} where it
331concerns 2-\ and bicategories: so in particular, our oplax natural
332transformations $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G$ have 2-cell components given by
333$\alpha_f \colon \alpha_B . Ff \Rightarrow Gf . \alpha_A$. We will tend to use
334either juxtaposition or the connective ``$.$'' to denote composition, relying
335on context to sort out precisely which sort of composition is intended. When it
336comes to tricategories, our primary references are \cite{GPS} and
337\cite{nicktricats}, but with a preference for the ``algebraic'' presentation of
338the latter: though we will not use this algebraicity in any essential way.
339We will also make use of \emph{pasting diagrams} of 2-cells inside
340bicategories. Such diagrams are only well-defined up to a choice of bracketing
341of their boundary, and so we assume such a choice to have been made wherever
342necessary. Occasionally we will need to use similar pasting diagrams of 2-cells
343in a tricategory, and the same caveat holds, only more so: here, the diagram is
344only well-defined up to a choice of order in which the pasting should be
345performed; and again, we assume such a choice to have been made. We adopt one
346further convention regarding pasting diagrams. Suppose we are given a 2-cell
347$\alpha \colon h(gf) \Rightarrow h'(g'f')$ in a bicategory $\B$, thus:
348\[
349\cd{
350& X \ar[r]^g & Y \ar[dr]^h \\
351W \ar[ur]^f \ar[dr]_{f'} \dtwocell{rrr}{\alpha} & & & Z\text, \\
352& X' \ar[r]_{g'} & Y' \ar[ur]_{h'}}
353\]
354together with a homomorphism of bicategories $F \colon \B \to \C$. Applying $F$
355to $\alpha$ yields a 2-cell $F(h(gf)) \Rightarrow F(h'(g'f'))$ of $\C$, but
356frequently, we will be more interested in the 2-cell
357\[
358\cd{
359& FX \ar[r]^{Fg} & FY \ar[dr]^{Fh} \\
360FW \ar[ur]^{Ff} \ar[dr]_{Ff'} \dtwocell{rrr}{} & & & FZ\text; \\
361& FX' \ar[r]_{Fg'} & FY' \ar[ur]_{Fh'}}
362\]
363obtained by pasting $F\alpha$ with suitable coherence constraints for the
364homomorphism $F$: and we will consistently denote the 2-cell obtained in this
365way by $\overline{F\alpha}$.
366\section{A bicategory of tricategories}\label{bicat-tricat}
367We begin by describing the lowest-dimensional structure into which
368tricategories and their homomorphisms can form themselves. At first, one might
369think that this would be a category; but unfortunately, composition of
370trihomomorphisms fails to be associative on the nose, as it requires one to
371compose 1-cells in a hom-bicategory, which is itself not an associative
372operation. Consequently, the best we can hope for is a \emph{bicategory} of
373tricategories, which we will denote by $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
374The simplest such bicategory would have trihomomorphisms as its 1-cells and
375\emph{blips} as its 2-cells. According to \cite{GPS}, blips are very degenerate
376tritransformations which can only exist between two trihomomorphisms $F, G
377\colon \S \to \T$ which agree on 0-, 1-,~2-\ and 3-cells. Though one might
378think that this forces $F$ and $G$ to be the same, they can in fact differ with
379respect to certain pieces of coherence data: and
380a ``blip'' is the
381means
382by which one measures these differences.
383However, if we are going to form a bicategory of tricategories, it may as well
384be the most general possible one; and so we will consider more general sorts of
385both 1-~and 2-cells. Let us begin by looking at the 1-cells.
386\begin{Defn}\label{laxhomom}
387Let $\S$ and $\T$ be tricategories.
388A \defn{lax homomorphism} $F \colon \S \to \T$ is a lax morphism of tricategories in the sense of \cite{GPS}, all of whose coherence 3-cells are invertible.
389Hence
390$F$ consists of:
391\begin{itemize}
392\item A function $F \colon \ob \S \to \ob \T$;
393\item Homomorphisms of bicategories $F_{A, B} \colon \S(A, B) \to \T(FA,
394FB)$;
395\item 2-cells $\iota_A \colon I_{FA} \to FI_A$;
396\item 2-cells $\chi_{f, g} \colon Fg.Ff \Rightarrow F(gf)$, pseudo-natural
397in $f$ and $g$;
398\item Invertible modifications $\omega$, $\delta$ and $\gamma$ witnessing
399the coherence of $\iota$ and $\chi$,
400\end{itemize}
401all subject to the axioms for a morphism of tricategories as found in
402\cite{GPS}.
403\end{Defn}
404The notion of lax homomorphism is a sensible one from many angles. We can
405compose lax homomorphisms just as we would compose homomorphisms of
406tricategories.
407If we are given a pair of monoidal bicategories \cite{monoidalbicats} which we view as one-object tricategories,
408then
409the lax homomorphisms between them are the natural bicategorical generalisation of a lax monoidal functor (\emph{weak monoidal homomorphisms}, in the terminology of \cite{monoidalbicats}).
410Lax homomorphisms from the terminal
411tricategory into $\T$ classify \emph{pseudomonads} in $\T$~--~that is, monads
412whose associativity and unit laws have been weakened to hold up to coherent
413isomorphism, and in a similar vein we may use lax homomorphisms to give a
414succinct definition of an \emph{enriched bicategory} in the sense of
415\cite{Carmody, Lack}~--~that is, of a bicategory ``enriched in a tricategory'',
416which is a one-dimension-higher version of a category enriched in a
417bicategory~\cite[Section 5.5]{bicats}, which is in turn a generalisation of the
418familiar notion of a category enriched in a monoidal category. We shall see a
419little more of enriched bicategories in Section~\ref{Sec:locallydouble}.
420We now turn to the 2-cells of $\cat{Tricat}_2$. The most informative precedent
421here is the corresponding notion one dimension down: the \emph{icons} of
422\cite{Lackicons, LP}. As mentioned in the Introduction, these are degenerate
423oplax transformations between homomorphisms of bicategories which agree on
4240-cells. To be precise, given two such homomorphisms of bicategories $F, G
425\colon \B \to \C$, an \defn{icon} $\alpha \colon F \To G$ is given by
426specifying for each 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\B$, a 2-cell $\alpha_f
427\colon Ff \To Gf$ of $\C$ such that:
428\begin{itemize}
429\item For each 2-cell $\sigma \colon f \To g$ of $\B$, the following
430diagram commutes:
431\[\cd{
432Ff \ar@2[r]^{\alpha_f} \ar@2[d]_{F \sigma} & Gf \ar@2[d]^{G \sigma} \\
433Fg \ar@2[r]_{\alpha_g} & Gg\text;
434}\]
435\item For each object $A \in \B$, the following diagram commutes:
436\[\cd{
437{\id_{FA}} \ar@2[r]^{\cong} \ar@{=}[d] & F\id_A \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{\id_A}} \\
438{\id_{GA}} \ar@2[r]_{\cong} & G\id_A\text;
439}\]
440\item For each pair of composable 1-cells $f \colon A \to B$, $g \colon B
441\to C$ in $\B$, the following diagram commutes:
442\[\cd{
443Fg . Ff \ar@2[r]^{\cong} \ar@2[d]_{\alpha_{g} . \alpha_{f}} & F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{gf}} \\
444Gg . Gf \ar@2[r]_{\cong} & G(gf)\text,
445}\]
446\end{itemize}
447where the arrows labelled with $\cong$ witness the pseudo-functoriality
448of $F$ and $G$. There is a bijection between icons $F \Rightarrow G$ and those
449oplax natural transformations $F \Rightarrow G$ whose components are all
450identities (hence the name: \emph{i}dentity \emph{c}omponent \emph{o}plax
451\emph{n}atural transformation); however, icons differ crucially from the oplax
452natural transformations representing them in regard to the manner of their
453\emph{composition}. Indeed, composition of oplax natural transformations is
454only associative up to invertible modification, whilst icons admit a strictly
455associative composition; and it is this which allows bicategories,
456homomorphisms and icons to form a $2$-category $\cat{Bicat}_2$.
457The 2-cells of $\cat{Tricat}_2$ we are about to describe~--~the
458\emph{ico-icons}~--~can be seen as higher-dimensional analogues of these
459bicategorical icons. They are doubly degenerate oplax tritransformations
460between lax trihomomorphisms which agree on both $0$- and $1$-cells. Here
461again, composition of ico-icons will not simply be composition of
462tritransformations, but rather a modified form of that composition which is
463\emph{strictly} associative. The choice of the name ico-icon will be explained
464by Proposition~\ref{embed} below.
465\begin{Defn}\label{icoicon}
466Given lax homomorphisms $F$, $G \colon \S \to \T$, an \defn{ico-icon} $\alpha
467\colon F \Rightarrow G$ may exist only if $F$ and $G$ agree on objects and
4681-cells of $\S$; and is then given by the following data:
469\begin{enumerate}[(TD1)]
470\item[(TD1)] For each pair of objects $A, B \in \S$, an icon
471\[\alpha_{A, B} \colon F_{A, B} \Rightarrow G_{A, B} \colon \S(A, B) \to \T(FA, FB)\]
472(so in particular, for each 2-cell $\theta \colon f \Rightarrow g$ of $\S$,
473a 3-cell of $\T$:
474\[\cd{
475Ff \ar@2[r]^{F \theta} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\alpha_{\theta}}& Fg \ar@{=}[d] \\
476Gf \ar@2[r]_{G \theta} & Gg
477}\quad\text{);}\]
478\item[(TD2)] For each object $A$ of $\S$, a 3-cell of $\T$:
479\[
480\cd{
481I_{FA} \ar@2[r]^{\iota^F_A} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{M^{\alpha}_A} & FI_A \ar@{=}[d] \\
482I_{GA} \ar@2[r]_{\iota^G_A} & GI_A\text;
483}\]
484\item[(TD3)] For each pair of composable 1-cells $f \colon A \to B$, $g
485\colon B \to C$ of $\S$, a 3-cell of $\T$:
486\[
487\cd{
488Fg . Ff \ar@2[r]^{\chi^F_{f, g}} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi^{\alpha}_{f, g}} & F(g f) \ar@{=}[d] \\
489Gg . Gf \ar@2[r]_{\chi^G_{f, g}} & G(g f)\text;
490}\]
491\end{enumerate}
492subject to the following axioms:
493\begin{enumerate}[(TA1)]
494\item[(TA1)] For each pair of 2-cells $\theta \colon f \Rightarrow g \colon
495B \to C$ and $\theta' \colon f' \Rightarrow g' \colon A \to B$ of $\S$,
496the following pasting equality holds:
497\[ \hphantom{=} \quad \cd[@!@-0.5em]{
498& Ff . Ff'
499\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[dl] \dlthreecell{d}{\Pi^{\alpha}}
500& F(ff')
501\ar@{=}[dl] \ar@2[dr]^{F(\theta \theta')} \dlthreecell{dd}{\alpha_{\theta \theta'}}
502\\ Gf . Gf'
503\ar@2[r]^{\chi^G} \ar@2[dr]_{G\theta . G\theta'}
504& G(ff')
505\ar@2[dr]^{G(\theta \theta')} \drthreecell{d}{\chi^G}
506& & F(g g')
507\ar@{=}[dl] \\
508& Gg . Gg'
509\ar@2[r]_{\chi^G}
510& G(gg')
511}\]\[ = \quad \cd[@!@-0.5em]{
512& Ff . Ff' \ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[dl] \ar@2[dr]_{F\theta . F\theta'}
513\dlthreecell{dd}{\alpha_\theta . \alpha_{\theta'}}
514& F(ff') \ar@2[dr]^{F(\theta \theta')} \drthreecell{d}{\chi^F}
515\\ Gf . Gf'
516\ar@2[dr]_{G\theta . G\theta'} & & Fg . Fg'
517\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[dl] \dlthreecell{d}{\Pi^\alpha} &
518F(gg')\text;
519\ar@{=}[dl] \\
520& Gg . Gg' \ar@2[r]_{\chi^G} & G(gg')\text. }\]
521\item[(TA2)] For each 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\S$, the following
522pasting equality holds:
523\[
524\hphantom{=} \quad \cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
525& FI_{B}.Ff
526\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \dthreecell{ddr}{\gamma^F}
527& F(I_B.f)
528\ar@2[dr]^{F\l}
529\\ I_{FB}.Ff
530\ar@2[dr]^{\l} \ar@2[ur]^{\iota^F.1} \ar@{=}[d]
531& & & Ff
532\ar@{=}[d]
533\\ I_{GB}.Gf
534\ar@2[dr]_{\l} \twoeq{r}
535& Ff
536\ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{dr}
537& Ff
538\ar@{=}[ur] \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{r}
539& Gf
540\\ & Gf
541\ar@{=}[r]
542& Gf
543\ar@{=}[ur]
544}\]
545\[
546= \quad \cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
547& FI_B . Ff
548\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi^\alpha}
549& F(I_B . f)
550\ar@2[dr]^{F\l} \ar@{=}[d]
551\\ I_{FB}.Ff
552\ar@2[ur]^{\iota^F.1} \ar@{=}[d] \ar@{}[r] \ar@3?(0.5)+/u 0.2cm/;?(0.5)+/d 0.2cm/_(1.5)*+[l]{\scriptstyle \ \ M^\alpha.1}
553& GI_B . Gf
554\ar@2[r]_{\chi^G} \dthreecell{ddr}{\gamma^G}
555& G(I_B . f)
556\ar@2[dr]_{G \l} \dthreecell{r}{\alpha_\l}
557& Ff
558\ar@{=}[d]
559\\ I_{GB}.Gf
560\ar@2[dr]_{\l} \ar@2[ur]_{\iota^G.1}
561& & & Gf\text.
562\\ & Gf
563\ar@{=}[r]
564& Gf
565\ar@{=}[ur]
566}\]
567\item[(TA3)] For each 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\S$, the following
568pasting equality holds:
569\[
570\hphantom{=} \quad \cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
571& Ff.FI_{A}
572\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \dthreecell{ddr}{\delta^F}
573& F(f.I_A)
574\ar@2[dr]^{F\r}
575\\ Ff.I_{FA}
576\ar@2[dr]^{\r} \ar@2[ur]^{1.\iota^F} \ar@{=}[d]
577& & & Ff
578\ar@{=}[d]
579\\ Gf.I_{GA}
580\ar@2[dr]_{\r} \twoeq{r}
581& Ff
582\ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{dr}
583& Ff
584\ar@{=}[ur] \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{r}
585& Gf
586\\ & Gf
587\ar@{=}[r]
588& Gf
589\ar@{=}[ur]
590}\]
591\[
592= \quad \cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
593& Ff.FI_A
594\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi^\alpha}
595& F(f.I_A)
596\ar@2[dr]^{F\r} \ar@{=}[d]
597\\ Ff.I_{FA}
598\ar@2[ur]^{1.\iota^F} \ar@{=}[d] \ar@{}[r] \ar@3?(0.5)+/u 0.2cm/;?(0.5)+/d 0.2cm/_(1.5)*+[l]{\scriptstyle \ \ 1.M^\alpha}
599& Gf.GI_A
600\ar@2[r]_{\chi^G} \dthreecell{ddr}{\delta^G}
601& G(f.I_A)
602\ar@2[dr]_{G \r} \dthreecell{r}{\alpha_\r}
603& Ff
604\ar@{=}[d]
605\\ Gf.I_{GA}
606\ar@2[dr]_{\r} \ar@2[ur]_{1.\iota^G}
607& & & Gf\text.
608\\ & Gf
609\ar@{=}[r]
610& Gf
611\ar@{=}[ur]
612}\]
613\item[(TA4)] For each triple $f, g, h$ of composable 1-cells of $\S$, the
614following pasting equality holds:
615\[
616\hphantom{=} \quad \cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
617& F(hg). Ff
618\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \dthreecell{ddr}{\omega^F}
619& F((hg)f)
620\ar@2[dr]^{F\a}
621\\ (Fh.Fg).Ff
622\ar@2[dr]^{\a} \ar@2[ur]^{\chi^F.1} \ar@{=}[d]
623& & & F(h(gf))
624\ar@{=}[d]
625\\ (Gh.Gg).Gf
626\ar@2[dr]_{\a} \twoeq{r}
627& Fh.(Fg. Ff)
628\ar@2[r]^{1. \chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{1.\Pi^\alpha}
629& Fh. F(gf)
630\ar@2[ur]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{r}{\Pi^\alpha}
631& G(h(gf))
632\\ & Gh.(Gg.Gf)
633\ar@2[r]_{1.\chi^G}
634& Gh.G(gf)
635\ar@2[ur]_{\chi^G}
636}\]
637\[
638= \quad \cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
639& F(hg). Ff
640\ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi^\alpha}
641& F((hg)f)
642\ar@2[dr]^{F\a} \ar@{=}[d]
643\\ (Fh.Fg).Ff
644\ar@2[ur]^{\chi^F.1} \ar@{=}[d] \ar@{}[r] \ar@3?(0.5)+/u 0.2cm/;?(0.5)+/d 0.2cm/_(1.5)*+[l]{\scriptstyle \ \ \Pi^\alpha.1}
645& G(hg).Gf
646\ar@2[r]_{\chi^G} \dthreecell{ddr}{\omega^G}
647& G((hg)f)
648\ar@2[dr]_{G \a} \dthreecell{r}{\alpha_\a}
649& F(h(gf))
650\ar@{=}[d]
651\\ (Gh.Gg).Gf
652\ar@2[dr]_{\a} \ar@2[ur]_{\chi^G.1}
653& & & G(h(gf))\text.
654\\ & Gh.(Gg.Gf)
655\ar@2[r]_{1.\chi^G}
656& Gh.G(gf)
657\ar@2[ur]_{\chi^G}
658}\]
659\end{enumerate}
660\end{Defn}
661Observe that, because the raw data for an ico-icon is a collection of 3-cells
662in the target tricategory, there is no possibility of introducing a third
663dimension of structure given by ``ico-icon modifications''. To do this we have
664to look at \emph{singly} degenerate, rather than \emph{doubly} degenerate,
665oplax tritransformations. We do this in the next Section.
666Now, in order to show that this collection of 0-, 1-~and 2-cells forms a
667bicategory, we have to give additional \emph{data}~--~vertical composition of
6682-cells, horizontal composition of 1-\ and 2-cells and associativity and
669unitality constraints~--~subject to additional \emph{axioms}~--~the category
670axioms for vertical composition, the middle-four interchange axiom and the
671pentagon and triangle axioms for the associativity and unit constraints.
672We start with the vertical structure: the identity 2-cell $\id_F \colon F
673\Rightarrow F$ in $\cat{Tricat}_2$ we take to be given by the following data:
674\[(\id_F)_{A, B} = \id_{F_{A, B}}\text, \quad
675M^{\id_F}_A = \id_{\iota^F_A} \quad \text{and} \quad \Pi^{\id_F}_{f, g} = \id_{\chi^F_{f, g}}
676\text.\] Each of the axioms (TA1)--(TA4) now expresses that something is equal to itself pasted
677together with some identity 3-cells, which is clear enough. Next, given 2-cells
678$\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G$ and $\beta \colon G \Rightarrow H$ in
679$\cat{Tricat}_2$, we take $\beta\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow H$ to be given by
680the following data:
681\[(\beta \alpha)_{A, B} = \beta_{A, B} . \alpha_{A, B}\text, \quad
682M^{\beta\alpha}_A = M^{\beta}_A . M^{\alpha}_A \quad \text{and} \quad \Pi^{\beta\alpha}_{f, g} =
683\Pi^{\beta}_{f, g} . \Pi^{\alpha}_{f, g}\text.\] Each of the axioms (TA1)--(TA4) for this data
684follow from juxtaposing the corresponding axioms for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in a
685very straightforward manner. Moreover, because vertical composition of 3-cells
686in a tricategory is strictly associative and unital, so is the vertical
687composition of 2-cells in $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
688We turn now to the horizontal structure. Horizontal identities and composition
689for 1-cells are the identities and composition for lax homomorphisms as
690detailed in \cite{Lack}; whilst given 2-cells $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow F'
691\colon \S \to \T$ and $\beta \colon G \Rightarrow G' \colon \T \to \U$, their
692horizontal composite $\beta \ast \alpha \colon GF \Rightarrow G'F' \colon \S
693\to \U$ is given by:
694\begin{enumerate}[(TD1)]
695\item[(TD1)] $(\beta \ast \alpha)_{A, B} := \beta_{A, B} \ast \alpha_{A,
696B}$, where $\ast$ on the right-hand side is the horizontal composite of
697the underlying icons in the 2-category $\cat{Bicat}_2$ of the
698Introduction. In particular, given a 2-cell $\theta \colon f
699\Rightarrow g$ of $\S$, we have
700\[(\beta \ast \alpha)_\theta \quad = \quad \cd{
701GFf \ar@2[r]^{GF \theta} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\beta_{F\theta}}& GFg \ar@{=}[d] \\
702G'Ff \ar@2[r]^{G'F \theta} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{G'\alpha_{\theta}}& G'Fg \ar@{=}[d] \\
703G'F'f \ar@2[r]_{G'F' \theta} & G'F'g\text{;}
704}\]
705\item[(TD2)]
706\[
707M^{\beta \ast \alpha}_A \quad := \quad \cd{
708I_{GFA}
709\ar@2[r]^{\iota^G} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{M^{\beta}_{FA}}
710& GI_{FA}
711\ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[r]^{G\iota^F} \dthreecell{dr}{\beta_{\iota^F}}
712& GFI_A
713\ar@{=}[d]
714\\ I_{G'FA}
715\ar@2[r]^{\iota^{G'}} \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{dr}
716& G'I_{FA}
717\ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[r]^{G'\iota^F} \dthreecell{dr}{G'M^{\alpha}_A}
718& G'FI_A
719\ar@{=}[d]
720\\ I_{G'F'A}
721\ar@2[r]_{\iota^{G'}}
722& G'I_{F'A}
723\ar@2[r]_{G'\iota^{F'}}
724& G'F'I_A\text,}
725\]
726\item[(TD3)]
727\[
728\Pi^{\beta \ast \alpha}_{f, g} \quad := \quad \cd{
729GFg . GFf
730\ar@2[r]^{\chi^G} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi^{\beta}_{Ff, Fg}}
731& G(Fg . Ff)
732\ar@2[r]^{G\chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\beta_{\chi^F}}
733& GF(gf)
734\ar@{=}[d] \\
735G'Fg . G'Ff
736\ar@2[r]^{\chi^{G'}} \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{dr}
737& G'(Fg . Ff)
738\ar@2[r]^{G'\chi^F} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{G'\Pi^\alpha_{f, g}}
739& G'F(gf)
740\ar@{=}[d] \\
741G'F'g . G'F'f
742\ar@2[r]_{\chi^{G'}}
743& G'(F'g . F'f)
744\ar@2[r]_{G'\chi^{F'}}
745& G'F'(gf)\text.
746}\]
747\end{enumerate}
748We must check that these data satisfy (TA1)--(TA4)\label{checkaxioms}.
749If we view the pasting equalities in these axioms as equating two ways round a cube or a hexagonal prism,
750then
751this verification is a matter of taking a suitable collection of such cubes and prisms for $\beta$ and $\alpha$ and sticking them together in the right way.
752When realised in two dimensions, this amounts to
753displaying a succession of equalities of rather large pasting diagrams. We
754leave the task of reconstructing these to the reader.
755Let us consider now the middle-four interchange axiom. Asking for this be
756satisfied amounts to checking that the other obvious way of defining $\beta
757\ast \alpha$~--~via $GF'$ rather than $G'F$~--~gives the same answer; and this
758follows quickly from the middle-four interchange law in the hom-bicategories of
759$\U$, and the first icon axiom for $\beta$.
760It remains to give the associativity and unit constraints $a$, $l$ and $r$ for
761$\cat{Tricat}_2$. For the left unit constraint $l$, consider a lax homomorphism
762$F \colon \S \to \T$, and write $F'$ for the composite $\id_\T.F \colon \S \to
763\T$. Now, $F'$ agrees with $F$ on 0-cells and on hom-bicategories, but differs
764in the remaining coherence data; indeed, we have
765\begin{align*}
766\iota^{F'}_{A} &= \cd{I_{FA} \ar@2[r]^-{\id_{I_{FA}}} & I_{FA} \ar@2[r]^-{\iota^F_{A}} &
767FI_A}\\
768\text{and} \quad \chi^{F'}_{f, g} &= \cd{Fg. Ff \ar@2[r]^-{\id_{Fg.Ff}} & Fg. Ff
769\ar@2[r]^-{\chi^F_{f, g}} & F(gf).}
770\end{align*}
771Thus we define a 2-cell $l_F \colon \id_\T . F \Rightarrow F$ in
772$\cat{Tricat}_2$ as follows:
773\begin{enumerate}[(TD1)]
774\item[(TD1)] $(l_F)_{A, B} = \id_{F_{A, B}} \colon {F_{A, B}} \Rightarrow
775{F_{A, B}}$;
776\item[(TD2)] $M^{l_F}_A$ is the unit isomorphism $\iota^F_A.(\id_{I_{FA}})
777\Rrightarrow \iota^F_A$ in the bicategory $\T(FA, FA)$;
778\item[(TD3)] $\Pi^{l_F}_{f, g}$ is the unit isomorphism $\chi^F_{f,
779g}.(\id_{Fg.Ff}) \Rrightarrow \chi^F_{f, g}$ in the bicategory $\T(FA,
780FC)$.
781\end{enumerate}
782Now each axiom (TA1)--(TA4) is a tautology which describes how we obtained
783$\chi^{F'}$, $\delta^{F'}$, $\gamma^{F'}$ and $\omega^{F'}$ from the
784corresponding data for $F$. The definition of $r$ is dual to that of $l$, so we
785pass over it and onto the associativity constraint $a$. Consider three lax
786homomorphisms $F \colon \R \to \S$, $G \colon \S \to \T$ and $H \colon \T \to
787\U$ and the two composites $(HG)F$ and $H(GF) \colon \R \to \U$. As above,
788these agree on 0-cells and on hom-bicategories (and so we write their common
789value simply as $HGF$) but differ with respect to coherence data. This time we
790have:
791\begin{align*}
792\iota^{(HG)F} &= HG\iota^F.(H\iota^G.\iota^H)\text, & \iota^{H(GF)} &=
793(HG\iota^F.H\iota^G).\iota^H\text,\\
794\chi^{(HG)F} &= HG\chi^F.(H\chi^G.\chi^H)\qquad\text{and} & \chi^{H(GF)} &=
795(HG\chi^F.H\chi^G).\chi^H\text,
796\end{align*}
797where we omit the subscripts for clarity.
798Thus
799we take $a_{F, G, H} \colon (HG)F \Rightarrow H(GF)$ in $\cat{Tricat}_2$ to be:
800\begin{enumerate}[(TD1)]
801\item[(TD1)] $(a_{F,G,H})_{A, B} = \id_{(HGF)_{A, B}} \colon (HGF)_{A, B}
802\Rightarrow (HGF)_{A, B}$;
803\item[(TD2)] $M^{a_{F,G,H}}_A$ is the associativity isomorphism
804\[HG\iota^F_A.(H\iota^G_{FA}.\iota^H_{GFA}) \Rrightarrow
805(HG\iota^F_A.H\iota^G_{FA}).\iota^H_{GFA}\] in the bicategory $\U(HGFA, HGFA)$;
806\item[(TD3)] $\Pi^{a_{F,G,H}}_{f, g}$ is the associativity isomorphism
807\[HG\chi^F_{f,g}.(H\chi^G_{Ff,Fg}.\chi^H_{GFf,GFg}) \Rrightarrow
808(HG\chi^F_{f,g}.H\chi^G_{Ff,Fg}).\chi^H_{GFf,GFg}\]
809in the bicategory $\U(HGFA, HGFC)$.
810\end{enumerate}
811We must now verify axioms (TA1)--(TA4) for these data. For this we observe that
812the 3-cell data $\chi$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\omega$ for $H(GF)$ and for
813$(HG)F$ are, in fact, obtained as different bracketings of the same pasting
814diagram.
815%for example, both $\omega^{H(GF)}_{f, g, h}$ and $\omega^{(HG)F}_{f, %g, h}$ are obtained as pastings of the diagram on the following page.
816So
817by the pasting theorem for bicategories, we can obtain the 3-cell data $\chi$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\omega$ for $H(GF)$ from that for $(HG)F$ by pasting with suitable associativity isomorphisms in the appropriate hom-bicategory of $\U$; and this is precisely what axioms (TA1)--(TA4) say.
818It remains to check the naturality of $l$, $r$ and $a$, and the pentagon and
819triangle identities. For the naturality of $l$, we must show that for any
8202-cell $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G$ of $\cat{Tricat}_2$, the following
821diagram commutes:
822\[\cd{
823{\id_\T} . F \ar@2[r]^{l_F} \ar@2[d]_{\id_\T . \alpha} & F \ar@2[d]^\alpha \\
824{\id_\T} . G \ar@2[r]_{l_G} & G\text.}
825\]
826We easily verify that the left-hand 2-cell $\alpha' = \id_\T . \alpha$ has
827components $\alpha'_\theta = \alpha_\theta$, $M^{\alpha'}_A =
828M^{\alpha}_A.(\id_{I_{FA}})$ and $\Pi^{\alpha'}_{f, g} = \Pi^{\alpha}_{f, g} .
829(\id_{Ff. Fg})$; therefore the naturality of $l$ is a consequence of the
830naturality of the left unit constraints in the hom-bicategories of $\T$; and
831dually for $r$. For the naturality of $a$, we must show that the following
832diagram commutes in $\cat{Tricat}_2$ for all suitable 2-cells $\alpha$, $\beta$
833and $\epsilon$:
834\[\cd{
835(HG)F \ar@2[r]^{a_{F,G,H}} \ar@2[d]_{(\alpha\beta)\epsilon} & H(GF) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha(\beta\epsilon)} \\
836(H'G')F' \ar@2[r]_{a_{F',G',H'}} & H'(G'F')\text,}
837\]
838for which we must show that (TD1)--(TD3) agree for the two ways around this
839square. For (TD1) this is trivial; so consider (TD2).
840For both $(\alpha \beta)\epsilon$ and $\alpha(\beta\epsilon)$, we obtain this datum by pasting together the same $3 \times 3$ diagram of 3-cells; the only difference being the manner in which we bracket together the boundary of this diagram.
841Thus
842the commutativity of the above square with respect to (TD2) is a further instance of the pasting theorem for bicategories.
843(TD3) is obtained in a similar manner.
844Finally, it is not hard to verify that the pentagon and triangle identities for
845$a$, $l$ and $r$ follow from instances of the pentagon and triangle identities
846in the hom-bicategories of the target tricategory. This completes the
847definition of the bicategory $\cat{Tricat}_2$.

922\section{Towards a tricategory of tricategories}\label{Sec:towards}
923We now wish to describe a tricategory of tricategories $\cat{Tricat}_3$. This
924will have the same 0-cells and
9251-cells as $\cat{Tricat}_2$, but will have 2-cells with one fewer level of degeneracy, which
926consequently
927admit a notion of 3-cell between them.
928Although we introduce the 2-~and 3-cells of
929$\cat{Tricat}_3$ in this Section, we will not actually prove that we obtain a
930tricategory from them until we reach Section~\ref{tritri}. As explained in the
931Introduction, we do this for two reasons. Firstly, so that we can set up some
932machinery which will allow us to avoid checking all the tricategorical
933coherence axioms by hand; and secondly, in order to investigate the curious
934fact that $\cat{Tricat}_3$ does not really extend $\cat{Tricat}_2$, in that not
935every $2$-cell of the latter gives rise to a $2$-cell of the former.
936We now begin our description of $\cat{Tricat}_3$. Its objects and $1$-cells
937are, as stated above, tricategories and lax trihomomorphisms. The $2$-cells are
938to be ``singly degenerate oplax tritransformations''. The most obvious way of
939interpreting this notion would be as follows:
940\begin{Defn}
941Let there be given lax homomorphisms of tricategories $F, G \colon \S \to \T$;
942then an
943\defn{oplax icon} $\alpha \colon F \Tor G$ may exist only if $F$ and $G$ agree on objects
944whereupon it consists of the following data:
945\begin{enumerate}[(ID1)]

947\[\alpha_{A, B} \colon F_{A, B} \Rightarrow G_{A, B} \colon \S(A, B) \to \T(FA,
948FB)\] (so in particular, for each 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\S$, we have a 2-cell $\alpha_f
949\colon Ff \Rightarrow Gf$ of $\T$, and for each 2-cell $\theta \colon f
950\Rightarrow g$ of $\S$, a 3-cell
951\[\cd{
952Ff \ar@2[r]^{F \theta} \ar@2[d]_{\alpha_f} \dthreecell{dr}{\alpha_{\theta}}& Fg \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_g} \\
953Gf \ar@2[r]_{G \theta} & Gg\quad \text{);}
954}\]
955\item[(ID2)] For each object $A$ of $\S$, a 3-cell of $\T$:
956\[

959I_{GA} \ar@2[r]_{\iota^G_A} & GI_A\text;

1123\end{Defn}
1124The definition of oplax icon generalises that of ico-icon, in that:
1125\begin{Prop}\label{embed} Let $F, G \colon \S \to \T$ be lax
1126homomorphisms. Then the ico-icons \mbox{$F \Rightarrow G$} are in bijection
1127with the class of oplax icons $\alpha \colon F \Tor G$ for which each component
1128$\alpha_f \colon Ff \Rightarrow Gf$ is an identity 2-cell: they are the
1129\emph{\underline{i}}dentity \emph{\underline{c}}omponents
1130\emph{\underline{o}}plax icons.
1131\end{Prop}
1132Unfortunately, oplax icons do not provide a suitable notion of 2-cell for our
1133tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$. The reason is that although oplax icons may be
1134``whiskered'' with lax homomorphisms on each side, these whiskerings do not
1135give rise to a well-defined composition of oplax icons along a 0-cell
1136boundary. Indeed, if we are given a diagram
1137\[\cd{
1138{\S} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{F} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{F'} \dtwocell{r}{\alpha} &
1139{\T} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{G} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{G'} \dtwocell{r}{\beta} &
1140{\U}
1141}\] of lax homomorphisms and oplax icons, then there are two canonical ways of
1142composing it up which need not agree, even up to isomorphism. The same
1143phenomenon occurs if one tries to form a tricategory of bicategories whose
11442-cells are oplax natural transformations. In order to obtain a tricategory, we
1145therefore restrict attention to a suitable subclass of the oplax icons:
1146\begin{Defn}\label{pseudoicon}
1147Let $F, G \colon \S \to \T$ be lax homomorphisms. By a \defn{pseudo-icon}
1148\mbox{$\alpha \colon F \Tor G$} we mean an oplax icon
1149$\alpha$ for which each 3-cell $\alpha_\theta$, $M^\alpha_A$, and
1150$\Pi^\alpha_{f, g}$ is invertible.
1151\end{Defn}
1152%Observe that a pseudo-icon is precisely what one gets by applying a naive
1153%dimension-raising to the notion of bicategorical icon: namely, inserting an
1154%invertible 3-cell into every diagram of 2-cells which previously commuted on
1155%the nose, and then subjecting all of this to an appropriate collection of
1156%axioms.
1157These pseudo-icons are to be the 2-cells of $\cat{Tricat}_3$. Note that,
1158although every ico-icon gives rise to an oplax icon, it is only the
1159\emph{invertible} ico-icons which give rise to pseudo-icons. We now turn to the
11603-cells of $\cat{Tricat}_3$.
1161\begin{Defn}\label{pseudoiconmod}
1162Given pseudo-icons $\alpha$, $\beta \colon F \Tor G$, a
1163\defn{pseudo-icon modification} \mbox{$\Gamma \colon \alpha \Rrightarrow
1164\beta$} consists in the following data:
1165\begin{enumerate}[(MD1)]
1166\item[(MD1)] For each $A, B$ in $\S$, a modification $\Gamma_{A, B} \colon
1167\alpha_{A, B} \Rrightarrow \beta_{A, B}$ (and so in particular, for
1168each
11691-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\S$, a
11703-cell $\Gamma_f \colon \alpha_f \Rrightarrow \beta_f$ of $\T$);
1171\end{enumerate}
1172subject to the following axioms:
1173\begin{enumerate}[(MA1)]
1174\item[(MA1)] For each object $A$ of $\S$, the following pasting equality
1175holds:
1176\[\cd[@u@!@+2em]{
1177I_{FA} \ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^{F}_A} &
1178I_{FA} \ar@2[dr]^{\iota^F_A} \\
1179I_{GA} \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^{G}_A} \dlthreecell{r}{M^{\beta}_A} &
1180FI_A \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{I_A}} \ar@{=}[r] \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_{I_A}} &
1181FI_A \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{I_A}}\\
1182& GI_A \ar@{=}[r] & GI_A
1183}\quad = \quad \cd[@u@!@+2em]{
1184I_{FA} \ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] &
1185I_{FA} \ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[dr]^{\iota^F_A} \\
1186I_{GA} \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^{G}_A} &
1187I_{GA} \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^G_A} \dlthreecell{r}{M^{\alpha}_A} &
1188FI_A \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{I_A}}\\
1189& GI_A \ar@{=}[r] & GI_A\text;
1190}
1191\]
1192\item[(MA2)] For each pair of composable 1-cells $f \colon A \to B$, $g
1193\colon B \to C$ of $\S$, the following pasting equality holds:
1194\end{enumerate}
1195\[\cd[@u@!@+2em@R-1em]{
1196Fg . Ff \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[d]_{\beta_g . \beta_f} \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^{F}_{f, g}} &
1197Fg . Ff \ar@2[dr]^{\chi^F_{f, g}} \\
1198Gg . Gf \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^{G}_{f, g}} \dlthreecell{r}{\Pi^{\beta}_{f, g}} &
1199F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{gf}} \ar@{=}[r] \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_{gf}} &
1200F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{gf}}\\
1201& G(gf) \ar@{=}[r] & G(gf)
1202}\quad = \quad \cd[@u@!@+2em@R-1em]{
1203Fg . Ff \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[d]_{\beta_g . \beta_f} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_g . \Gamma_f} &
1204Fg . Ff \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_g . \alpha_f} \ar@2[dr]^{\chi^F_{f, g}} \\
1205Gg . Gf \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^{G}_{f, g}} &
1206Gg . Gf \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^G_{f, g}} \dlthreecell{r}{\Pi^{\alpha}_{f, g}} &
1207F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{gf}}\\
1208& G(gf) \ar@{=}[r] & G(gf)\text.

1210\]
1211\end{Defn}
1212\begin{Thm}\label{mainresultprop}
1213There is a tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$ with objects being tricategories;
1214\mbox{1-cells}, lax homomorphisms; 2-cells, pseudo-icons; and 3-cells,
1215pseudo-icon modifications.
1216\end{Thm}
1217It would certainly be possible to prove this result at this point in the paper:
1218we would simply follow the same path as in Section~\ref{bicat-tricat}, first
1219defining the various kinds of composition we need, then the various pieces of
1220coherence data, and finally checking the coherence axioms these must satisfy.
1221However, rather than doing this directly, we would like to reuse some of the
1222results we proved about $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
1223Indeed, we have already shown that that the composition of lax homomorphisms is
1224associative up to an invertible ico-icon. Each invertible ico-icon witnessing this
1225associativity gives rise to a corresponding pseudo-icon in $\cat{Tricat}_3$;
1226and so by taking these pseudo-icons as our witnesses for associativity in
1227$\cat{Tricat}_3$, we might hope to be able to reuse the coherence work we did
1228in Section~\ref{bicat-tricat}.
1229However, matters are not quite this simple.
1230If we take the unique sensible definition of vertical composition of pseudo-icons,
1231then
1232we find that the composition of two invertible ico-icons \emph{qua} ico-icon does not agree with their composite \emph{qua} pseudo-icon.
1233In particular, the invertible ico-icons
1234witnessing associativity in $\cat{Tricat}_2$ become mere equivalence
1235pseudo-icons in $\cat{Tricat}_3$, whilst each commutative diagram of coherence
12362-cells in $\cat{Tricat}_2$ gives rise to a diagram in $\cat{Tricat}_3$ which
1237may commute only up to an invertible 3-cell.
1238Intuitively, it is clear that this should not be a problem, and that we should
1239still be able to ``read off'' the coherence for $\cat{Tricat}_3$ from that for
1240$\cat{Tricat}_2$, but to make this precise we must turn our intuition into a
1241mathematical principle. In order to motivate how we will do this, let us
1242examine more closely why the naive approach does not work.
1243The problem is essentially that the putative tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$ does not include
1244\emph{all} of the data carried by the mere bicategory $\cat{Tricat}_2$. This occurs at the
1245level of basic cell data~--~since not every ico-icon is a pseudo-icon~--~but more importantly,
1246at the level of compositional data: the data for the strictly associative composition of
1247ico-icons from $\cat{Tricat}_2$ is no longer present in $\cat{Tricat}_3$.
1248The solution we give to this problem is to describe a categorical structure into which
1249tricategories, lax homomorphisms, pseudo-icons and modifications may be formed which is richer
1250than $\cat{Tricat}_3$, and in particular retains \emph{all} the data from $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
1251This categorical structure is not a tricategory, but rather what we call a \emph{locally
1252cubical bicategory}. This is a genuinely weak three-dimensional structure whose coherence laws
1253are particularly simple: they have a bicategorical rather than tricategorical flavour. In
1254particular, the locally cubical bicategory of tricategories that we construct will be able to
1255take its coherence data directly from $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
1256The existence of the desired tricategory of tricategories $\cat{Tricat}_3$ now
1257follows from
1258a general result (given in Section~\ref{Sec:fromltt}) which says that any well-behaved locally cubical bicategory gives rise to a tricategory in a canonical way.
1259This result can be seen as a crystallisation of the intuition
1260we had above that we should be able to ``read off'' the coherence of
1261$\cat{Tricat}_3$ from $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
