1289\section{Locally cubical bicategories}\label{Sec:locallydouble}
1290The purpose of this section is to define the locally cubical bicategories
1291alluded to at the end of the previous section. Like tricategories, these are
1292weak categorical structures comprised of 0-, 1-, 2-~and 3-cells; however, the
12932-cells come in two varieties, \emph{horizontal} and \emph{vertical}, whilst
1294the 3-cells are cubical in nature. Composition of vertical 2-cells is strictly
1295associative; that of horizontal 2-cells is only so up to an invertible 3-cell;
1296whilst the associativity constraints for 1-cells are given by \emph{vertical}
12972-cells, and are of a bicategorical, up-to-isomorphism, rather than a
1298tricategorical, up-to-equivalence, kind. A locally cubical bicategory may be
1299described succinctly as a ``bicategory weakly enriched in pseudo double
1300categories''; and our task in this section will be to expand upon this
1301description.
1302The concept of \emph{strict} double
1303category is due to Ehresmann.
1304It is an example of the notion of \emph{double model} for an essentially-algebraic theory, this being a model of the theory in its own category of ($\cat{Set}$-based) models.
1305Thus
1306a double category~--~which is a double model of the theory of categories~--~is a category object in $\cat{Cat}$.
1307The theory
1308of categories is somewhat special, since its category of ($\cat{Set}$-based)
1309models may be enriched to a 2-category, so that, as well as \emph{strict}
1310category objects in $\cat{Cat}$, we may also consider \emph{pseudo} category
1311objects: and these are the pseudo double categories which we will be interested
1312in.
1313\begin{Defn}
1314A \defn{pseudo double category}~\cite{GP1} $\mathfrak C$ is given by specifying
1315a collection of \emph{objects} $x, y, z, \dots$, a collection of \emph{vertical
13161-cells} between objects, which we write as $a \colon x \to y$, a collection of
1317\emph{horizontal 1-cells} between objects, which we write as $f \colon x \tor
1318y$, and a collection of \emph{2-cells}, each of which is bounded by a square of
1319horizontal and vertical arrows, and which we write as:
1320\[\cd{
1321x \ar[d]_{a} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{f} \dtwocell{dr}{\alpha}& w \ar[d]^{b} \\
1322y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{g} & z\text,}\] or sometimes simply as $\alpha \colon f \Rightarrow g$.
1323Moreover, we must give:
1324\begin{itemize}
1325\item Identities and composition for vertical 1-cells, $\id_x \colon x \to
1326x$ and $(a, b) \mapsto ab$, making the objects and vertical arrows into
1327a category $\C_0$;
1328\item Vertical identities and composition for 2-cells, $\id_{f} \colon f
1329\Rightarrow f$ and $(\beta, \alpha) \mapsto \beta \alpha$:
1330\[\cd{
1331x \ar[d]_{\id_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{f} \dtwocell{dr}{\id_{f}}& y \ar[d]^{\id_y} \\
1332x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{f} & y} \quad \text; \quad \cd{
1333u \ar[d]_{a} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{f} \dtwocell{dr}{\alpha}& x \ar[d]^{b} \\
1334v \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{g} \ar[d]_{c} \dtwocell{dr}{\beta}& y \ar[d]^{d} \\
1335w \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{h} & z} \mapsto
1336\cd{u \ar[d]_{ca} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{f} \dtwocell{dr}{\beta\alpha}& x \ar[d]^{db} \\
1337w \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{h} & z}
1338\]
1339making the horizontal arrows and 2-cells into a category $\C_1$ for which
1340``vertical source'' and ``vertical target'' become functors $s, t \colon
1341\C_1 \to \C_0$;
1342\item Identities and composition for horizontal 1-cells, $\DI x \colon x
1343\tor x$ and $(g, f) \mapsto gf$;
1344\item Horizontal identities and composition for 2-cells, $\DI a \colon \DI
1345x \Rightarrow \DI y$ and $(\beta, \alpha) \mapsto \beta \ast \alpha$:
1346\[\cd{
1347x \ar[d]_{a} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\DI x} \dtwocell{dr}{\DI a}& x \ar[d]^{a} \\
1348y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\DI y} & y} \quad \text; \quad \cd{
1349u \ar[d]_{a} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{f} \dtwocell{dr}{\alpha}& v \ar[d]^{b} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{g} \dtwocell{dr}{\beta} & w \ar[d]^{c} \\
1350x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{h} & y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{k} & z} \mapsto
1351\cd{u \ar[d]_{a} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{gf} \dtwocell{dr}{\beta \ast \alpha}& w \ar[d]^{c} \\
1352x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{kh} & z\text,}
1353\]
1354satisfying functoriality constraints: firstly, $\DI{(\thg)}$ is a functor
1355$\C_0 \to \C_1$, which says that $\DI{\id_x} = \id_{\DI x}$ and $\DI{ab} =
1356\DI a.\DI b$ and secondly, horizontal composition is a functor
1357$\mathord{\ast} \colon \C_1 \smt \C_1 \to \C_1$ which says that $\id_{g}
1358\ast \id_{f} = \id_{gf}$ and $(\delta \ast \gamma).(\beta \ast \alpha) =
1359(\delta \beta) \ast (\gamma \alpha)$.
1360\item Horizontal unitality and associativity constraints given by 2-cells
1361\[\cd{
1362x \ar[d]_{\id_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\DI y.f} \dtwocell{dr}{\l_{f}}& y \ar[d]^{\id_y} \\
1363x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{f} & y}\text, \quad \cd{
1364x \ar[d]_{\id_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{{f}.\DI x} \dtwocell{dr}{\r_{f}}& y \ar[d]^{\id_y} \\
1365x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{f} & y}\text, \quad \text{and} \quad \cd[@C+1.5em]{
1366x \ar[d]_{\id_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{h(gf)} \dtwocell{dr}{\a_{f,g,h}}& z \ar[d]^{\id_z} \\
1367x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{(hg)f} & z\text,}
1368\]
1369natural in $f$, $g$ and $h$, and invertible as arrows of $\C_1$. These
13702-cells must obey two laws: the pentagon law, which equates the two routes
1371from $k(h(gf))$ to $((kh)g)f$, and the triangle law, which equates the two
1372routes from $g.(\DI y.f)$ to $gf$.
1373\end{itemize}
1374\end{Defn}
1375Pseudo double categories are sometimes also known as \emph{weak} double
1376categories; they are a special case of Verity's more general notion of
1377\emph{double bicategory}~\cite{dv}. A more comprehensive reference on pseudo
1378double categories is \cite{GP1}: though be aware that we interchange its usage
1379of the terms ``horizontal'' and ``vertical'' to give a better fit with the
1380usual \mbox{2-categorical} terminology. Since the only sorts of double
1381categories we will be concerned with in this paper are the pseudo ones, we may
1382sometimes choose to write simply ``double category'', leaving the qualifier
1383``pseudo'' understood.
1384Some simple examples of pseudo double categories are $\mathfrak{Cat}$, the pseudo double
1385category of ``categories, functors, profunctors and transformations'', $\mathfrak{Rng}$, the
1386pseudo double category of ``rings, ring homomorphisms, bimodules and skew-linear maps'', and
1387the pseudo double category $\mathfrak{Span}(\C)$ of ``objects, morphisms, spans and span
1388morphisms'' in a category with pullbacks $\C$. These are typical examples of pseudo double
1389categories, in that they have notions of \emph{homomorphism} and \emph{bimodule} as their
1390respective vertical and horizontal 1-cells. Any bicategory $\B$ gives us a pseudo double
1391category $\UU(\B)$ with only identity vertical 1-cells, whilst any pseudo double category
1392$\mathfrak C$ gives a bicategory $\HH(\mathfrak C)$ upon throwing away the non-identity
1393vertical 1-cells, and all the 2-cells except for those whose vertical source and target are
1394identity arrows. We will refer to such 2-cells as \defn{globular 2-cells}; they are also
1395sometimes known as \emph{special} 2-cells.
1396Just as in the theory of bicategories, the appropriate notion of morphism
1397between pseudo double categories only preserves horizontal composition up to
1398comparison 2-cells, the most important case being the \emph{homomorphisms}, for
1399which these 2-cells are invertible. We can define a homomorphism between small
1400pseudo double categories in terms of a pseudomorphism of pseudocategory
1401objects, but just as easy is to give the elementary description:
1402\begin{Defn}
1403A \defn{homomorphism of pseudo double categories} $F \colon \mathfrak C \to
1404\mathfrak D$ is given by assignations on objects, 1-cells and 2-cells which
1405preserve source and target and are functorial with respect to vertical
1406composition of 1-\ and 2-cells, together with comparison 2-cells
1407\[\cd{
1408{Fx} \ar[d]_{\id_{F x}} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\DI{Fx}} \dtwocell{dr}{\mathfrak m_{x}}& {F x} \ar[d]^{\id_{F x}} \\
1409Fx \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{F\DI x} & Fx} \quad \text{and} \quad \cd{
1410{F x} \ar[d]_{\id_{F x}} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{F g. F f} \dtwocell{dr}{\mathfrak m_{f, g}}& {F z} \ar[d]^{\id_{F z}} \\
1411Fx \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{F (g f)} & Fz}
1412\]
1413which are invertible as arrows of $\D_1$, and natural in $x$, respectively $g$
1414and $f$. Moreover, we require the commutativity of three familiar diagrams,
1415which equate, respectively, the two possible ways of going from $Ff.\DI{Fx}$ to
1416$Ff$, from $\DI{Fy}. Ff$ to $Ff$, and from $Fh.(Fg.Ff)$ to $F((hg)f)$.
1417\end{Defn}
1418With the obvious notion of composition and identities, we obtain a category
1419$\cat{DblCat}$ of (possibly large) pseudo double categories and homomorphisms
1420between them. If we write $\cat{Bicat}$ for the category of bicategories and
1421homomorphisms,
1422then
1423the assignations $\B \mapsto \UU(\B)$ and $\mathfrak C
1424\mapsto \HH(\mathfrak C)$ described above extend to a pair of adjoint functors
1425\mbox{$\UU \dashv \HH \colon \cat{DblCat} \to \cat{Bicat}$}, for which the
1426composite $\HH\UU$ is the identity; we can thus view $\cat{Bicat}$ as a
1427coreflective subcategory of $\cat{DblCat}$.
1428Now, $\cat{DblCat}$ is in fact the underlying ordinary category of a 2-category
1429whose 2-cells are the so-called \emph{vertical transformations}. We can
1430understand these 2-cells by observing that there is a 2-monad on the
14312-category \mbox{$\cat{CatGph} := [\,\bullet \rightrightarrows \bullet, \,
1432\cat{Cat}]$} whose strict algebras are small pseudo double categories, and
1433whose algebra pseudomorphisms are the homomorphisms between them. The
1434corresponding \emph{algebra 2-cells} are precisely the vertical
1435transformations. Spelling this out, we have:
1436\begin{Defn}
1437A \defn{vertical transformation} $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G$ between
1438homomorphisms of pseudo double categories $F, G \colon \mathfrak C \to
1439\mathfrak D$ is given by specifying, for each object $x \in \mathfrak C$, a
1440vertical 1-cell $\alpha_x \colon Fx \to Gx$ of $\mathfrak D$ and for each
1441horizontal 1-cell $f \colon x \tor y$ in $\mathfrak C$ a 2-cell
1442\[\cd{
1443Fx \ar[d]_{\alpha_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{Ff} \dtwocell{dr}{\alpha_f}& Fy \ar[d]^{\alpha_y} \\
1444Gx \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{Gf} & Gy}\] of $\mathfrak D$, such that the $\alpha_x$'s are natural in
1445morphisms of $\D_0$, the $\alpha_f$'s are natural in morphisms of $\D_1$, and
1446the following diagrams commute:
1447\[\cd{
1448\DI{Fx} \ar@2[r]^{\mathfrak m^F_x} \ar@2[d]_{\DI{\alpha_x}} & F\DI x \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{\DI x}} \\
1449\DI{Gx} \ar@2[r]_-{\mathfrak m^G_x} & G\DI x
1450} \quad \text{and} \quad
1451\cd{ Fg.Ff \ar@2[r]^{\mathfrak m^F_{g, f}} \ar@2[d]_{\alpha_g \ast \alpha_f} & F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{gf}} \\
1452Gg.Gf \ar@2[r]_-{\mathfrak m^G_{g, f}} & G(gf)\text.}
1453\]
1454\end{Defn}
1455In the case that $\mathfrak C$ and $\mathfrak D$ are bicategories, the vertical
1456transformation between homomorphisms $\mathfrak C \to \mathfrak D$ are
1457precisely the bicategorical icons of Section 1; however, the reader should
1458carefully note that the coreflection of $\cat{DblCat}$ into $\cat{Bicat}$ does
1459\emph{not} enrich to a two-dimensional coreflection, since there is no way of
1460coreflecting a general vertical transformation between homomorphisms of pseudo
1461double categories into an icon between the corresponding homomorphisms of
1462bicategories.
1463It follows from the algebraic description of $\cat{DblCat}$ that it admits a
1464wide class of 2-dimensional limits, of which we will only be concerned with
1465finite products.
1466That $\cat{DblCat}$ admits these, makes it, of course, into a symmetric monoidal category, but the 2-dimensional aspect of these products
1467means that
1468we may view it instead as a \emph{symmetric monoidal 2-category}: that is, a symmetric monoidal category whose tensor product is a 2-functor and whose coherence natural transformations are 2-natural transformations.
1469What we
1470now wish to describe is how we can use this monoidal 2-category $\cat{DblCat}$
1471as a suitable base for \emph{enrichment}.
1472For any monoidal category $\V$, we have the well-known notion of a \emph{category enriched in
1473$\V$} or \emph{$\V$-category}, which instead of having hom-sets between 0-cells, has
1474hom-objects drawn from $\V$, with the corresponding composition being expressed by morphisms
1475of $\V$ subject to associativity and unitality laws. Now, if instead of a monoidal category
1476$\V$ we begin with a \emph{monoidal bicategory} $\W$ in the sense of \cite{monoidalbicats},
1477then we may generalise this definition to obtain the notion of \emph{bicategory enriched in
1478$\W$} or \mbox{\emph{$\W$-bicategory}}~\cite{Carmody, Lack}. A $\W$-bicategory is like a
1479bicategory, but instead of hom-categories between 0-cells, it has hom-objects drawn from $\W$:
1480and instead of composition functors, it has composition morphisms drawn from $\W$, which are
1481now required to be associative and unital only up to coherent 2-cells of $\W$.\footnote{Note
1482that this differs from the notion of ``category enriched in a bicategory'' studied in
1483\cite{Enrichedbicats}; these are the \emph{polyads} of \cite{bicats}, and are essentially
1484categories enriched in a monoidal category where that monoidal category happens to be spread
1485out over many objects.}\ \ Thus we can think of a $\W$-bicategory as being a ``category
1486weakly enriched in $\W$''.
1487The simplest sort of enriched bicategory is a $\cat{Cat}$-bicategory, which is
1488just a (\mbox{locally} small) ordinary bicategory. Other examples are obtained
1489by taking \mbox{$\W = \cat{\V}\text-\cat{Cat}$} for some monoidal category
1490$\V$, for which a $\W$-bicategory has sets of 0-\ and 1-\ cells as usual, but
1491now a $\V$-object of 2-cells between any parallel pair of 1-cells; by taking
1492$\W = \cat{Mod}$, the bicategory of categories and profunctors, for which a
1493$\W$-bicategory is a \emph{probicategory} in the sense of Day \cite{Biclosed};
1494and by taking $\W$ to be an ordinary monoidal category, viewed as a locally
1495discrete monoidal bicategory, whereupon $\W$-bicategories reduce to categories
1496enriched in $\W$. An account of the general theory of enriched bicategories can
1497be found in \cite{Lack}, but we will need sufficiently little of it that we can
1498easily arrange for our account to be self-contained:
1499\begin{Defn}
1500A \defn{locally cubical bicategory} is a bicategory enriched in the monoidal
15012-category $\cat{DblCat}$. Explicitly, it is given by the following data:
1502\begin{enumerate}[(LDD1)]
1503\item[(LDD1)] A collection $\ob {\mathfrak B}$ of objects;
1504\item[(LDD2)] For every pair $A, B \in \ob {\mathfrak B}$, a pseudo double
1505category ${\mathfrak B}(A, B)$;
1506\item[(LDD3)] For every $A \in \ob {\mathfrak B}$, a unit homomorphism
1507\[\elt{I_x} \colon 1 \to {\mathfrak B}(A, A)\text;\]
1508\item[(LDD4)] For every triple $A, B, C \in \ob {\mathfrak B}$, a
1509composition homomorphism
1510\[\otimes \colon {\mathfrak B}(B, C) \times {\mathfrak B}(A, B) \to {\mathfrak B}(A, C)\text;\]
1511\item[(LDD5)] For every pair $A, B \in \ob {\mathfrak B}$, invertible
1512vertical transformations
1513\[\cd[@C+1em]{
1514{\mathfrak B}(A, B) \times {\mathfrak B}(A, A) \ar[dr]_{\otimes} & {\mathfrak B}(A, B) \rtwocell[0.36]{dl}{r}
1515\ltwocello[0.36]{dr}{l} \ar[r]^-{\elt{I_B} \times 1} \ar[l]_-{1 \times \elt{I_A}} \ar[d]_{1} &
1516{\mathfrak B}(B, B) \times {\mathfrak B}(A, B)\text; \ar[dl]^{\otimes} \\ & {\mathfrak B}(A, B) & {}
1517}\]
1518\item[(LDD6)] For every quadruple $A, B, C, D \in \ob {\mathfrak B}$, an
1519invertible vertical transformation
1520\[\cd[@C+1em]{
1521{\mathfrak B}(C, D) \times {\mathfrak B}(B, C) \times {\mathfrak B}(A, B) \ar[d]_{\otimes \times 1} \ar[r]^-{1 \times \otimes}
1522\dtwocell{dr}{a} &
1523{\mathfrak B}(C, D) \times {\mathfrak B}(A, C) \ar[d]^{\otimes}\\
1524{\mathfrak B}(B, D) \times {\mathfrak B}(A, B) \ar[r]_-{\otimes} & {\mathfrak B}(A, D)\text.}\]
1525\end{enumerate}
1526Subject to the following two axioms:
1527\begin{enumerate}[(LDA1)]
1528\item[(LDA1)] For each triple of objects $A, B, C$ of ${\mathfrak B}$, the
1529following pasting equality holds:
1530\[\cd[@+1em@C+1em]{
1531{\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]^{1 \times \elt{I_B} \times 1} \ar[d]_{1} \dtwocell{dr}{1 \times l} & {\mathfrak B}^3 \ar[r]^{1 \times \otimes} \ar[d]^{1 \times \otimes} & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[d]^{\otimes}\\
1532{\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]_1 & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]_{\otimes} & {\mathfrak B}
1533} \quad = \quad \cd[@+1em@C+1em]{
1534{\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]^{1 \times \elt{I_B} \times 1} \ar[d]_{1} \dtwocell{dr}{r \times 1} & {\mathfrak B}^3 \ar[r]^{1 \times \otimes} \ar[d]^{\otimes \times 1} \dtwocell{dr}{a} & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[d]^{\otimes}\\
1535{\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]_1 & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]_{\otimes} & {\mathfrak
1536B}\text, }\] where $\mathfrak B^2$ and $\mathfrak B^3$ abbreviate the appropriate products of hom-double categories;
1537\item[(LDA2)] For each quintuple of objects $A, B, C, D, E$ of ${\mathfrak
1538B}$, the following pasting equality holds:
1539\[
1540\cd[@!@+1em]{
1541{\mathfrak B}^4 \ar[r]^{1 \times 1 \times \otimes} \ar[d]_{\otimes\times 1\times 1} \twocong{dr} & {\mathfrak B}^3 \ar[dr]^{1 \times \otimes} \ar[d]^{\otimes \times 1}\\
1542{\mathfrak B}^3 \ar[r]_{1 \times \otimes} \ar[dr]_{\otimes \times 1} & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[dr]^{\otimes} \drtwocell{d}{a} \dtwocell{r}{a} & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[d]^{\otimes} \\
1543& {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]_{\otimes} & {\mathfrak B}
1544} \quad = \quad \cd[@!@+1em]{
1545{\mathfrak B}^4 \ar[r]^{1 \times 1 \times \otimes} \ar[dr]|{1 \times \otimes \times 1} \ar[d]_{\otimes\times 1\times 1} & {\mathfrak B}^3 \ar[dr]^{1 \times \otimes} \drtwocell{d}{1 \times a}\\
1546{\mathfrak B}^3 \ar[dr]_{\otimes \times 1} \drtwocell[0.4]{r}{a \times 1} & {\mathfrak B}^3 \dtwocell{dr}{a} \ar[d]^{\otimes \times 1} \ar[r]_{1 \times \otimes} & {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[d]^{\otimes} \\
1547& {\mathfrak B}^2 \ar[r]_{\otimes} & {\mathfrak B}\text,
1548}
1549\]
1550where we observe the same convention regarding $\mathfrak B^4$, $\mathfrak
1551B^3$ and $\mathfrak B^2$.
1552\end{enumerate}
1553\end{Defn}
1554It may be helpful to extract a description of the various sorts of composition
1555that a $\cat{DblCat}$-bicategory possesses. The 0-cells, 1-cells and vertical
15562-cells form an ordinary bicategory. Next come the the horizontal 2-cells,
1557which can be composed with each other along either a 1-cell boundary or a
15580-cell boundary, with both compositions being associative up to an invertible
1559globular 3-cell; moreover, the corresponding ``middle four interchange'' law
1560only holds up to an invertible globular 3-cell. Finally, the 3-cells themselves
1561can be composed with each other along the two different types of 2-cell
1562boundary and along 0-cell boundaries; and these operations are strictly
1563associative modulo the associativity of the boundaries.
1564A \emph{one-object} locally cubical bicategory amounts to a
1565\defn{monoidal double category} \cite{doubleclubs,GP2,mike}~--~that is, a pseudo double category with an
1566up-to-isomorphism tensor product on it. In particular, any double category with \emph{finite
1567products} in the appropriate double categorical sense\footnote{By which we mean a
1568\emph{pseudo-functorial choice of double products} in the sense of \cite{GP1}. Such pseudo
1569double categories are slightly stricter versions of the \emph{cartesian bicategories} of
1570\cite{cb2}, which, although they are presented in a globular way, are essentially cubical
1571structures.}\ \ becomes a monoidal double category under the cartesian tensor product. The
1572double categories $\mathfrak{Cat}$, $\mathfrak{Span}(\C)$ (where $\C$ is a category with
1573finite limits) and $\mathfrak{Rng}$ are all monoidal in this way: though in the case of
1574$\mathfrak{Rng}$, there is another natural monoidal structure which is derived from the tensor
1575product on the category of rings.
1576For a non-degenerate example of a locally cubical bicategory, we turn to
1577$\cat{DblCat}$ itself. As demonstrated in \cite{doubleclubs}, we may define an
1578internal hom 2-functor
1579\[\HOM{\, \thg , ?} \colon \cat{DblCat}^\op \times
1580\cat{DblCat} \to \cat{DblCat}\label{hom}\] for which $\HOM{\mathfrak C, \mathfrak D}$ is the
1581following double category. Its objects are homomorphisms $\mathfrak C \to \mathfrak D$, and
1582its vertical 1-cells $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G$ are the vertical transformations between
1583them. Its horizontal 1-cells $\alpha \colon F \Tor G$ are the \emph{horizontal pseudo-natural
1584transformations}, whose components at an object $x \in \mathfrak C$ are given by horizontal
15851-cells $\alpha_x \colon Fx \tor Gx$ of $\mathfrak D$, together with pseudo-naturality data
1586like that for a pseudo-natural transformation of bicategories; and indeed, in the case that
1587$\mathfrak C$ and $\mathfrak D$ are bicategories the two notions coincide. Finally, the
15882-cells of $\HOM{\mathfrak C, \mathfrak D}$ are the \emph{cubical modifications}, which are
1589bounded by two horizontal and two vertical transformations and whose basic data consists of
1590giving, for each object of the source, a 2-cell of the target bounded by the components of
1591these transformations: Definition \ref{cubbicat} below makes this explicit in the special case
1592where $\mathfrak C$ and $\mathfrak D$ are bicategories.
1593When we say that $\HOM{\thg, ?}$ acts as an internal hom, we are affirming a
1594universal property: namely, that for each $\mathfrak C$ the 2-functor $(\thg)
1595\times \mathfrak C \colon \cat{DblCat} \to \cat{DblCat}$ is left biadjoint to
1596$\HOM{\, \mathfrak C, \thg}$, so that what we have is a \emph{biclosed}
1597monoidal bicategory in the sense of \cite{monoidalbicats}. Now, in \cite{Lack},
1598it is demonstrated that, just as any closed monoidal category can be viewed as
1599a category enriched over itself, so any biclosed monoidal bicategory can be
1600viewed as a bicategory enriched over itself, with the hom-objects being given
1601by the biclosed structure. Applying this result to the monoidal 2-category
1602$\cat{DblCat}$, we obtain a locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{DblCat}$,
1603with 0-cells being the pseudo double categories; 1-cells, the homomorphisms;
1604vertical 2-cells, the vertical transformations; horizontal 2-cells, the
1605horizontal pseudo-natural transformations; and 3-cells the cubical
1606modifications.
1607In particular, if we restrict our attention to those pseudo double categories
1608lying in the image of the embedding $\mathbb U \colon \cat{Bicat} \to
1609\cat{DblCat}$ then we obtain:
1610\begin{Cor}\label{bicategories-as-dblcatbicategories}
1611There is a locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Bicat}$ which has as 0-cells,
1612bicategories; as 1-cells, homomorphisms; as vertical 2-cells, bicategorical
1613icons; as horizontal 2-cells, pseudo-natural transformations; and as 3-cells,
1614cubical modifications.
1615\end{Cor}
1616Whilst the 0-, 1-, and 2-cells of $\mathfrak{Bicat}$ are familiar, the same is not true of the
16173-cells; and since we will need them in Definition~\ref{cubicalpseudo} below, it is worth
1618giving an explicit description.
1619\begin{Defn}\label{cubbicat}
1620Suppose that $F, G, H, K \colon \B \to \C$ are homomorphisms of bicategories;
1621that \mbox{$\alpha \colon F \Tor G$} and $\beta \colon H \Tor K$ are
1622pseudo-natural transformations; and that \mbox{$\gamma \colon F \Rightarrow H$}
1623and $\delta \colon G \Rightarrow K$ are bicategorical icons. Then a
1624\defn{cubical modification}
1625\[\cd{
1626F \ar@2[d]_{\gamma} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma}& G \ar@2[d]^{\delta} \\
1627H \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\beta} & K}\] is given by specifying, for every
1628object $A \in \B$ a 2-cell $\Gamma_A \colon \alpha_A \Rightarrow \beta_A$, in
1629such a way that for every 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\B$, the following
1630pasting equality holds:
1631\[ \cd[@!]{
1632& FB
1633\ar[r]^{\alpha_B} \rtwocell{d}{\alpha_f} \ar@{<-}[dl]_{Ff}
1634& GB
1635\ar@{=}[d] \ar@{<-}[dl]|{Gf} \\
1636FA
1637\ar[r]^{\alpha_A} \ar@{=}[d] \dtwocell{dr}{\Gamma_A}
1638& GA
1639\ar@{=}[d] \dtwocell{r}{\delta_f}
1640& KB
1641\ar@{<-}[dl]^{Kf}
1642\\ HA
1643\ar[r]_{\beta_A}
1644& KA\text;
1645} \quad = \quad \cd[@!]{
1646& FB
1647\ar[r]^{\alpha_B} \ar@{=}[d] \dtwocell{dr}{\Gamma_B} \ar@{<-}[dl]_{Ff}
1648& GB
1649\ar@{=}[d] \\
1650FA
1651\ar@{=}[d] \dtwocell{r}{\gamma_f}
1652& HB
1653\ar[r]_{\beta_B} \ar@{<-}[dl]|{Hf} \rtwocell{d}{\beta_f}
1654& KB
1655\ar@{<-}[dl]^{Kf}
1656\\ HA
1657\ar[r]_{\beta_A}
1658& KA\text.
1659}\]
1660\end{Defn}
1661In particular, to give a \emph{globular} 3-cell of $\mathfrak{Bicat}$ is
1662precisely to give a modification between pseudo-natural transformations in the
1663standard sense; and so $\mathfrak{Bicat}$ is rich enough to encode faithfully
1664all the cells and all of the forms of composition which feature in the
1665tricategory of bicategories, but is able to do so using coherence whose
1666complexity does not rise above the bicategorical level.
1667Pleasing as this is, we should note that not every tricategory can be reduced
1668to a locally cubical bicategory in this way; for example, given a bicategory
1669$\B$ with bipullbacks, we may form the tricategory $\cat{Span}(\B)$ of spans in
1670$\B$. In this tricategory, 1-cell composition is given by bipullback, and so is
1671only determined up-to-equivalence, rather than up-to-isomorphism; so evidently,
1672it will be inexpressible as a locally cubical bicategory.
1673\begin{Rk}
1674There are two canonical ways of forming a tricategory of bicategories,
1675corresponding to the two canonical ways of composing a pair of strong
1676transformations along a 0-cell boundary: however, Proposition
1677\ref{bicategories-as-dblcatbicategories} exhibited a single canonical locally
1678cubical bicategory of bicategories. The discrepancy is resolved if we observe
1679that to obtain this $\cat{DblCat}$-bicategory we must fix a choice of biclosed
1680structure on $\cat{DblCat}$, and that there are two canonical ways of doing
1681this, depending on how we choose the counit maps $\HOM{\mathfrak B, \mathfrak
1682C} \times \mathfrak B \to \mathfrak C$ for the biadjunctions in question.
1683\end{Rk}
1684\section{A locally cubical bicategory of tricategories}\label{Sec:local} We now
1685return to our study of tricategories with the goal of forming them into a
1686locally cubical bicategory. The result we will prove in this section is:
1687\begin{Thm}\label{loccubtricat}
1688There is a locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$ with 0-cells being
1689tricategories; 1-cells, lax homomorphisms; vertical 2-cells, ico-icons;
1690horizontal 2-cells, pseudo-icons; and 3-cells, cubical pseudo-icon
1691modifications.
1692\end{Thm}
1693We have already met the lax homomorphisms (Definition \ref{laxhomom}), the
1694ico-icons (Definition \ref{icoicon}) and the pseudo-icons (Definition
1695\ref{pseudoicon}); however, we have not yet introduced the \emph{cubical
1696pseudo-icon modifications}. These generalise the (globular) pseudo-icon
1697modifications of Definition \ref{pseudoiconmod} as follows:
1698\begin{Defn}\label{cubicalpseudo}
1699Let $F$, $G$, $F'$, $G' \colon \S \to \T$ be lax homomorphisms of
1700tricategories, let $\alpha \colon F \Tor G$ and $\beta \colon F' \Tor G'$ be
1701pseudo-icons, and let $\gamma \colon F \Rightarrow F'$ and $\delta \colon G
1702\Rightarrow G'$ be ico-icons. Then a
1703\defn{cubical pseudo-icon modification}\vskip-\baselineskip
1704\[\cd{
1705F \ar@2[d]_{\gamma} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma}& G \ar@2[d]^{\delta} \\
1706F' \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\beta} & G'}\] consists in the following data:
1707\begin{enumerate}[(MD1)]
1708\item[(MD1)] For each $A, B$ in $\S$, a cubical modification (cf.
1709Definition \ref{cubbicat})\vskip-\baselineskip
1710\[\cd{
1711F_{A, B} \ar@2[d]_{\gamma_{A, B}} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha_{A, B}} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_{A, B}}& G_{A, B} \ar@2[d]^{\delta_{A, B}} \\
1712F'_{A, B} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\beta_{A, B}} & G'_{A, B}}\] (and so in
1713particular, for each 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\S$, a
17143-cell $\Gamma_f \colon \alpha_f \Rrightarrow \beta_f$ of $\T$);
1715\end{enumerate}
1716subject to the following axioms:
1717\begin{enumerate}[(MA1)]
1718\item[(MA1)] For each object $A$ of $\S$, the following pasting equality
1719holds:
1720\[\cd[@u@!@+1em]{
1721I_{F'A} \ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^{F'}_A} &
1722I_{FA} \ar@2[dr]^{\iota^F_A} \dthreecell[0.45]{d}{M^{\gamma}_A} \\
1723I_{G'A} \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^{G'}_A} \dlthreecell{r}{M^{\beta}_A} &
1724F'I_A \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{I_A}} \ar@{=}[r] \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_{I_A}} &
1725FI_A \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{I_A}}\\
1726& G'I_A \ar@{=}[r] & GI_A
1727}\quad = \quad \cd[@u@!@+1em]{
1728I_{F'A} \ar@{=}[r] \ar@{=}[d] &
1729I_{FA} \ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[dr]^{\iota^F_A} \\
1730I_{G'A} \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^{G'}_A} &
1731I_{GA} \ar@2[dr]_{\iota^G_A} \dlthreecell{r}{M^{\alpha}_A} \dthreecell[0.45]{d}{M^{\delta}_A} &
1732FI_A \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{I_A}}\\
1733& G'I_A \ar@{=}[r] & GI_A\text;
1734}
1735\]
1736\item[(MA2)] For each pair of composable 1-cells $f \colon A \to B$, $g
1737\colon B \to C$ of $\S$, the following pasting equality holds:
1738\end{enumerate}
1739\[\cd[@u@!@+1.5em@R-1em]{
1740F'g . F'f \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[d]_{\beta_g . \beta_f} \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^{F'}_{f, g}} &
1741Fg . Ff \ar@2[dr]^{\chi^F_{f, g}} \dthreecell{d}{\Pi^{\gamma}_{f, g}} \\
1742G'g . G'f \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^{G'}_{f, g}} \dlthreecell{r}{\Pi^{\beta}_{f, g}} &
1743F'(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{gf}} \ar@{=}[r] \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_{gf}} &
1744F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{gf}}\\
1745& G'(gf) \ar@{=}[r] & G(gf)
1746}\quad = \quad \cd[@u@!@+1.5em@R-1em]{
1747F'g . F'f \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[d]_{\beta_g . \beta_f} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_g . \Gamma_f} &
1748Fg . Ff \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_g . \alpha_f} \ar@2[dr]^{\chi^F_{f, g}} \\
1749G'g . G'f \ar@{=}[r] \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^{G'}_{f, g}} &
1750Gg . Gf \ar@2[dr]_{\chi^G_{f, g}} \dlthreecell{r}{\Pi^{\alpha}_{f, g}} \dthreecell[0.45]{d}{\Pi^{\delta}_{f, g}} &
1751F(gf) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{gf}}\\
1752& G'(gf) \ar@{=}[r] & G(gf)\text.
1753}
1754\]
1755\end{Defn}
1756\noindent The first step in the proof of Theorem \ref{loccubtricat} will be to
1757give the local structure:
1758\begin{Prop}\label{localstruct}
1759Let $\S$ and $\T$ be tricategories. Then the lax homomorphisms, ico-icons,
1760pseudo-icons and cubical pseudo-icon modifications from $\S$ to $\T$ form a
1761pseudo double category $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$.
1762\end{Prop}
1763\begin{proof}
1764Underlying each lax homomorphism, ico-icon, pseudo-icon or cubical pseudo-icon
1765modification is an indexed family of homomorphisms of bicategories,
1766bicategorical icons, pseudo-natural transformations, or cubical modifications,
1767respectively: thus our approach will be to lift the compositional structure
1768from the pseudo double categories $\HOM{\mathfrak C, \mathfrak D}$ as defined
1769preceding Corollary~\ref{bicategories-as-dblcatbicategories}.
1770We begin with the vertical structure of $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$.
1771We have already seen in Section~\ref{bicat-tricat} that the lax homomorphisms and ico-icons from $\S$ to $\T$ form a category; we must show the same is true of the pseudo-icons and the cubical pseudo-icon modifications.
1772So
1773for each pseudo-icon $\alpha \colon F \Tor G$ we must give a cubical pseudo-icon modification \[\cd{ F \ar@2[d]_{\id_F} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\id_{\alpha}}& G \ar@2[d]^{\id_G} \\ F \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\alpha} & G\text;}\] which we take to be given by the identity family of cubical
1774modifications $(\id_\alpha)_{A, B} = \id_{\alpha_{A, B}} \colon \alpha_{A, B} \Rrightarrow \alpha_{A, B}$.
1775The axioms (MA1) and (MA2) are clear, since every occurence of $\Gamma$
1776reduces to an identity 3-cell. Next, given cubical pseudo-icon modifications
1777\[\cd{
1778F \ar@2[d]_{\sigma} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma}& F' \ar@2[d]^{\sigma'} \\
1779G \ar@2[d]_{\tau} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\beta} \dthreecell{dr}{\Delta}& G' \ar@2[d]^{\tau'} \\
1780H \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\gamma} & H'\text;}\]
1781we must provide a vertical composite $\Delta\Gamma \colon \alpha \Rrightarrow \gamma$, which
1782we do by composing their underlying families of cubical modifications:
1783\[(\Delta\Gamma)_{A, B} = \Delta_{A, B}. \Gamma_{A, B} \colon \alpha_{A, B} \Rrightarrow \gamma_{A, B}\text.\]
1784Now the axioms (MA1) and (MA2) follow from an application of the corresponding
1785axiom for $\Delta$ followed by the corresponding axiom for $\Gamma$.
1786Associativity and unitality of this composition follow from that for
1787composition of cubical modifications.
1788We next describe the horizontal identities of $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$. Firstly, for each
1789lax homomorphism $F \colon \S \to \T$, we must give an identity pseudo-icon $\DI F \colon F
1790\Tor F$. This has (ID1) given by the family $(\DI F)_{A, B} = \id_{F_{A, B}} \colon F_{A, B}
1791\Rightarrow F_{A, B}$ whilst $M^{\DI F}_A$ and $\Pi^{\DI F}_{A, B, C}$ are given by unnamed
1792coherence isomorphisms in the hom-bicategories of $\T$. Secondly, for each ico-icon $\alpha
1793\colon F \Rightarrow G$, we must give a cubical pseudo-icon modification
1794\[\cd{
1795F \ar@2[d]_{\alpha} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\DI F} \dthreecell{dr}{\DI \alpha}& F \ar@2[d]^{\alpha} \\
1796G \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\DI G} & G\text;}\] which we do by taking (MD1) to be given by the identity family of cubical
1797modifications $\id_{\id_{Ff}} \colon \id_{Ff} \Rrightarrow \id_{Gf}$. Each of the axioms
1798(IA1)--(IA3) for $\DI F$ and (MA1)--(MA2) for $\DI \alpha$ now asserts that some 3-cell is
1799equal to itself when pasted with such unnamed coherence cells, and this follows from coherence
1800for bicategories. Finally, we must check functoriality of $\DI{(\thg)}$, which is immediate.
1801We now come to the horizontal composition of $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$. First, for each
1802pair of pseudo-icons $\alpha \colon F \Tor G$ and $\beta \colon G \Tor H$, we must give a
1803composite pseudo-icon $\beta \alpha \colon F \Tor H$. We do this as follows:
1804\begin{enumerate}[(ID1)]
1805\item[(ID1)] $(\beta\alpha)_{A, B} = \beta_{A, B}.\alpha_{A, B} \colon
1806F_{A, B} \Rightarrow H_{A, B}$;
1807\item[(ID2)] $M^{\beta\alpha}_A$ is the pasting:
1808\[
1809\cd[@C+1em]{
1810I_{FA} \ar@2[r]^{\iota^F_A} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{M^{\alpha}_A} & FI_A \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{I_A}} \\
1811I_{GA} \ar@2[r]|{\iota^G_A} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{M^{\beta}_A} & GI_A \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{I_A}} \\
1812I_{HA} \ar@2[r]_{\iota^H_A} & HI_A\text;
1813}\]
1814\item[(ID3)] $\Pi^\alpha_{A, B, C}$ is the pasting:
1815\[
1816\cd{
1817F(\thg) \otimes F(?) \ar@2[r]^{\chi^F} \ar@2[d]|{\alpha_{(\thg)}\otimes \alpha_{(?)}} \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi_{A, B, C}^\alpha} \ar@/_5em/@2[dd]_{(\beta\alpha)_{(\thg)} \otimes (\beta\alpha)_{(?)}} &
1818F\big((\thg) \otimes (?)\big) \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{((\thg) \otimes (?))}} \\
1819G(\thg)\otimes G(?) \twocong[-0.4]{r} \ar@2[r]^{\chi^G} \ar@2[d]|{\beta_{(\thg)}\otimes \beta_{(?)}} \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi_{A, B, C}^\beta} &
1820G\big((\thg) \otimes (?)\big) \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{((\thg) \otimes (?))}} \\
1821H(\thg)\otimes H(?) \ar@2[r]_{\chi^H} &
1822H\big((\thg) \otimes (?)\big)\text.
1823}
1824\]
1825\end{enumerate}
1826Showing that these data satisfy axioms (IA1)--(IA3) is almost as simple as
1827placing the corresponding diagrams for $\beta$ and $\alpha$ alongside each
1828other; though not quite, since there are a number of auxiliary coherence
1829results we need to prove first. For instance, in order to prove (IA1) we must
1830show that:
1831\begin{multline*}
1832\cd{
1833I_{FB} . Ff \ar@2[r]^{\iota^F .1} \ar@2[d]|{1 . \alpha_f} \dthreecell{dr}{\overline{M^\alpha . 1}} \ar@/_5em/@2[dd]_{1 . (\beta\alpha)_f} &
1834FI_B . Ff \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_{I_B} . \alpha_f} \ar@/^5em/@2[dd]^{(\beta\alpha)_{I_B} . (\beta\alpha)_f}\\
1835I_{GB} . Gf \twocong[-0.4]{r} \ar@2[r]^{\iota^G .1} \ar@2[d]|{1 . \beta_f} \dthreecell{dr}{\overline{M^\beta . 1}} &
1836GI_B . Gf \twocong[-0.4]{l} \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{I_B} . \beta_f} \\
1837I_{HB} . Hf \ar@2[r]_{\iota^H . 1} &
1838HI_B . Hf
1839} \\ = \quad \cd[@+1em]{
1840I_{FB} . Ff \ar@2[r]^{\iota^F .1} \ar@2[d]_{1 . (\beta\alpha)_f} \dthreecell{dr}{\overline{M^{\beta\alpha} .
18411}} &
1842FI_B . Ff \ar@2[d]^{(\beta\alpha)_{I_B} . (\beta\alpha)_f} \\
1843I_{HB} . Hf \ar@2[r]_{\iota^H .1} &
1844HI_B . Hf\text;
1845}
1846\end{multline*}
1847holds; and similarly for (IA2) and (IA3). These derivations are straightforward
1848bicategorical manipulations and left to the reader.
1849Secondly, for each diagram of cubical pseudo-icon modifications
1850\[\cd{
1851F \ar@2[d]_{\sigma} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma}& G\ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\beta} \dthreecell{dr}{\Delta} \ar@2[d]^{\tau} & H \ar@2[d]^{\upsilon} \\
1852F' \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\alpha'} & G' \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\beta'} & H'}\] we must
1853give a cubical pseudo-icon modification $\Delta \ast \Gamma \colon \beta \alpha \Rrightarrow
1854\beta' \alpha' \colon F \Rightarrow H$. We do this by taking
1855\[(\Delta \ast \Gamma)_{A, B} = \Delta_{A, B} \ast \Gamma_{A, B} \colon
1856\beta_{A, B} \alpha_{A, B} \Rrightarrow \beta'_{A, B}. \alpha'_{A, B}\text,\] where $\ast$ on
1857the right-hand side is horizontal composition of cubical modifications in the pseudo double
1858category $\HOM{\S(A, B), \T(FA, FB)}$. Explicitly, for any 1-cell $f$ of the tricategory $\S$,
1859the 3-cell $(\Delta \ast \Gamma)_f$ of the tricategory $\T$ is given by the pasting
1860\[\cd[@u]{
1861Ff \ar@2[d]_{\alpha'_f} \ar@{=}[r] \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma_f} & Ff \ar@2[d]^{\alpha_f}\\
1862Gf \ar@2[d]_{\beta'_f} \ar@{=}[r] \dthreecell{dr}{\Delta_f} & Gf \ar@2[d]^{\beta_f}\\
1863Hf \ar@{=}[r] & Hf\text,
1864}\] and thus (MA1) and (MA2) for $\Delta \ast \Gamma$ follow by placing the corresponding
1865axioms for $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ beside each other, together with some very simple
1866manipulation with unnamed coherence cells. Finally, we must check functoriality of the
1867horizontal composition functor, which is just the middle-four interchange law. This will hold
1868in $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$ because it does in each double category $\HOM{\S(A, B),
1869\T(FA, FB)}$.
1870It remains only to give the unitality and associativity constraints for the pseudo double category $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$.
1871So
1872let there be given pseudo-icons $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G$, $\beta \colon G \Rightarrow H$ and $\gamma \colon H \Rightarrow K$.
1873Then:
1874\begin{itemize}
1875\item The associativity constraint $\a_{\alpha, \beta, \gamma} \colon
1876(\gamma\beta)\alpha \Rrightarrow \gamma(\beta\alpha)$ has component
1877modification $(\a_{\alpha, \beta, \gamma})_{A, B}$ given by the
1878associativity constraint $\a_{\alpha_{A, B}, \beta_{A, B}, \gamma_{A,
1879B}}$ in the double category $\HOM{\S(A, B), \T(FA, FB)}$;
1880\item The left unitality constraint $\l_\alpha \colon \id_G . \alpha
1881\Rrightarrow \alpha$ has component modification $(\l_\alpha)_{A, B}$
1882given by the left unitality constraint $\l_{\alpha_{A, B}}$ in
1883$\HOM{\S(A, B), \T(FA, FB)}$;
1884\item The right unitality constraint $\r_\alpha \colon \alpha . \id_G
1885\Rrightarrow \alpha$ has component modification $(\r_\alpha)_{A, B}$
1886given by the right unitality constraint $\r_{\alpha_{A, B}}$ in
1887$\HOM{\S(A, B), \T(FA, FB)}$.
1888\end{itemize}
1889The naturality of these constraints in $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ is
1890inherited from the hom-double categories $\HOM{\S(A, B), \T(FA, FB)}$; and that
1891these data satisfy the axioms (MA1) and (MA2) is also straightforward. In the
1892case of $\a_{\alpha, \beta, \gamma}$, for example, we see that $M^{\gamma(
1893\beta\alpha)}_A$ and $\Pi^{\gamma(\beta\alpha)}_{f, g}$ can be obtained from
1894$M^{(\gamma \beta) \alpha}_A$ and $\Pi^{(\gamma\beta)\alpha}_{f, g}$ by pasting
1895with unnamed coherence isomorphisms; but the components of $\a_{\alpha, \beta,
1896\gamma}$ are built from the selfsame coherence isomorphisms, and so the result
1897follows from the coherence theorem for bicategories.
1898\end{proof}
1899In order for the pseudo double categories $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$ we have
1900just defined to provide homs for the locally cubical bicategory
1901$\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$, we must define double homomorphisms which provide
1902top-level identities and composition. The double homomorphism
1903\[\elt{I_\T} \colon 1 \to \mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\T, \T)\] is straightforward; it sends the unique object of the terminal pseudo double category
1904to the identity lax homomorphism $\id_\T \colon \T \to \T$, the unique vertical 1-cell to the
1905identity ico-icon on $\id_T$; the unique horizontal 1-cell to the identity pseudo-icon on
1906$\id_\T$; and the unique 2-cell to the identity cubical pseudo-icon modification on this. The
1907coherence data for this homomorphism is obtained from unitality constraints in
1908$\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\T, \T)$, and so the homomorphism axioms follow from coherence for
1909bicategories. We must now give the composition double homomorphism
1910\[\otimes \colon \mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\T, \U) \times \mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T) \to \mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \U)\text.\]
1911The general approach to defining this will be similar to that adopted in the proof of
1912Proposition \ref{localstruct}. There, we defined the compositional structure on
1913$\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$ by lifting it from the pseudo double categories $\HOM{\S(A, B),
1914\T(FA, FB)}$: here, we will define $\otimes$ by lifting the double homomorphisms
1915\begin{multline*}
1916\HOM{\T(FA, FB), \U(GFA, GFB)} \times \HOM{\S(A, B), \T(FA,
1917FB)} \\ \longrightarrow \ \HOM{\S(A, B), \U(GFA, GFB)}
1918\end{multline*}
1919which provide composition in the locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Bicat}$ of Proposition
1920\ref{bicategories-as-dblcatbicategories}.
1921In detail, $\otimes$ is given as follows. On objects and vertical 1-cells, it
1922is given by the composition law for $\cat{Tricat}_2$. On horizontal 1-cells, we
1923consider pseudo-icons \mbox{$\alpha \colon F \Tor F' \colon \S \to \T$} and
1924$\beta \colon G \Tor G' \colon \T \to \U$, for which the composite pseudo-icon
1925$\beta \otimes \alpha \colon GF \Tor G'F'$ is given as follows:
1926\begin{enumerate}[(ID1)]
1927\item[(ID1)] $(\beta \otimes \alpha)_{A, B} = \beta_{FA, FB} \otimes
1928\alpha_{A, B}$, where $\otimes$ on the right-hand side is one of the
1929two canonical choices for horizontal composition of pseudo-natural
1930transformations; for concreteness let us take
1931\[(\beta \otimes \alpha)_f = \cd{GFf \ar@2[r]^{\beta_{Ff}} & G'Ff \ar@2[r]^{G'\alpha_f} & G'F'f}\]
1932and
1933\[(\beta \otimes \alpha)_\theta \quad = \quad \cd{
1934GFf \ar@2[r]^{GF \theta} \ar@2[d]_{\beta_{Ff}} \dthreecell{dr}{\beta_{F\theta}}& GFg \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{Fg}} \\
1935G'Ff \ar@2[r]^{G'F \theta} \ar@2[d]_{G'\alpha_f} \dthreecell{dr}{G'\alpha_{\theta}}& G'Fg \ar@2[d]^{G'\alpha_g} \\
1936G'F'f \ar@2[r]_{G'F' \theta} & G'F'g\text{;}
1937}\]
1938\item[(ID2)] $M^{\beta \otimes \alpha}_A$ is the following 3-cell:
1939\[\cd{
1940I_{GFA}
1941\ar@2[r]^{\iota^G} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{M^{\beta}_{FA}}
1942& GI_{FA}
1943\ar@2[d]^{\beta_{I_{FA}}} \ar@2[r]^{G\iota^F} \dthreecell{dr}{\beta_{\iota^F}}
1944& GFI_A
1945\ar@2[d]^{\beta_{FI_A}}
1946\\ I_{G'FA}
1947\ar@2[r]^{\iota^{G'}} \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{dr}
1948& G'I_{FA}
1949\ar@{=}[d] \ar@2[r]^{G'\iota^F} \dthreecell{dr}{\overline{G'M^{\alpha}_A}}
1950& G'FI_A
1951\ar@2[d]^{G'\alpha_{I_A}}
1952\\ I_{G'F'A}
1953\ar@2[r]_{\iota^{G'}}
1954& G'I_{F'A}
1955\ar@2[r]_{G'\iota^{F'}}
1956& G'F'I_A\text;}
1957\]
1958\item[(ID3)] $\Pi^{\beta \otimes \alpha}_{A, B, C}$ is the pseudo-natural
1959transformation with the following components:
1960\[
1961\cd[@C+1em]{
1962GFg . GFf
1963\ar@/_5em/@2[dd]_{(\beta \otimes \alpha)_g . (\beta \otimes \alpha)_f} \ar@2[r]^{\chi^G} \ar@2[d]|{\beta_{Fg} . \beta_{Ff}} \dthreecell{dr}{\Pi^{\beta}_{Ff, Fg}}
1964& G(Fg . Ff)
1965\ar@2[r]^{G\chi^F} \ar@2[d]^{\beta_{Fg . Ff}} \dthreecell{dr}{\beta_{\chi^F}}
1966& GF(gf)
1967\ar@2[d]^{\beta_{F(gf)}} \\
1968G'Fg . G'Ff \twocong[-0.4]{r}
1969\ar@2[r]^{\chi^{G'}} \ar@2[d]|{G'\alpha_g . G'\alpha_f} \twocong{dr}
1970& G'(Fg . Ff)
1971\ar@2[r]^{G'\chi^F} \ar@2[d]|{G'(\alpha_g . \alpha_f)} \dthreecell{dr}{\overline{G'\Pi^\alpha_{f, g}}}
1972& G'F(gf)
1973\ar@2[d]^{G'\alpha_{gf}} \\
1974G'F'g . G'F'f
1975\ar@2[r]_{\chi^{G'}}
1976& G'(F'g . F'f)
1977\ar@2[r]_{G'\chi^{F'}}
1978& G'F'(gf)\text.
1979}\]
1980\end{enumerate}
1981The proof that these data satisfy axioms (IA1)--(IA3) consists once again in
1982building large cubes or hexagonal prisms from smaller ones, together with some
1983simple manipulation with unnamed coherence cells: and once again, we leave this
1984task to the reader.
1985Finally we must define the action of $\otimes$ on pseudo-icon modifications.
1986Given two such:
1987\[
1988\cd{
1989F \ar@2[d]_{\sigma} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\Gamma}& F' \ar@2[d]^{\sigma'} \\
1990H \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\gamma} & H'
1991} \quad \text{and} \quad \cd{
1992G \ar@2[d]_{\tau} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\beta} \dthreecell{dr}{\Delta}& G' \ar@2[d]^{\tau'} \\
1993K \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\delta} & K'
1994}
1995\]
1996in the hom-double categories $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$ and
1997$\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\T, \U)$ respectively, we define their composite
1998\mbox{$\Delta \otimes \Gamma \colon \beta \otimes \alpha \Rrightarrow \delta
1999\otimes \gamma$} to be given by horizontally composing their underlying
2000families of cubical modifications in the locally cubical bicategory
2001$\mathfrak{Bicat}$:
2002\[(\Delta \otimes \Gamma)_{A, B} = \Gamma_{FA, FB} \otimes
2003\Delta_{A, B} \colon \beta_{FA, FB} \otimes \alpha_{A, B}
2004\Rrightarrow \delta_{FA, FB} \otimes \gamma_{A, B}\text.\] So in
2005particular, for any 1-cell $f \colon A \to B$ of $\S$, we have $(\Delta \otimes
2006\Gamma)_f$ given by the following pasting
2007\[\cd{
2008GFf \ar@2[r]^{\beta_{Ff}} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\Delta_{Ff}} &
2009G'Ff \ar@2[r]^{G'\alpha_{f}} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{\tau'_{\alpha_f}} &
2010G'F'f \ar@{=}[d] \\
2011KFf \ar@2[r]^{\delta_{Ff}} \ar@{=}[d] \twoeq{dr} &
2012K'Ff \ar@2[r]^{K'\alpha_{f}} \ar@{=}[d] \dthreecell{dr}{K'\Gamma_f} &
2013K'F'f \ar@{=}[d] \\
2014KHf \ar@2[r]_{\delta_{Hf}} &
2015K'Hf \ar@2[r]_{K'\gamma_{f}} &
2016K'H'f\text.}\]
2017Proving axioms (MA1) and (MA2) for this data amounts to constructing a further
2018succession of pasting equalities which traverse the interior of a $2 \times 2
2019\times 2$ cube, using:
2020\begin{itemize}
2021\item the corresponding axioms (MA1) or (MA2) for $\Delta$ and $\Gamma$,
2022\item the cubical modification axioms for the components of $\Delta$,
2023\item the icon axioms for the components of $\tau'$,
2024\item the pseudo-natural transformation axioms for the components of
2025$\delta$,
2026\item and some further calculus with unnamed coherence isomorphisms.
2027\end{itemize}
2028Functoriality of this composition with respect to vertical composition is
2029inherited from that of horizontal composition of cubical modifications in
2030$\mathfrak{Bicat}$.
2031It remains to exhibit the pseudo-functoriality constraints for $\otimes$; so
2032let there be given lax homomorphisms and pseudo-icons
2033\[\cd{
2034\S \ar@/^2em/[rr]^{F} \ar[rr]|{F'} \ar@/_2em/[rr]_{F''} & {}\dtwocell[0.36]{d}{\gamma} \dtwocell[-0.36]{d}{\alpha} &
2035\T \ar@/^2em/[rr]^{G} \ar[rr]|{G'} \ar@/_2em/[rr]_{G''} & {}\dtwocell[0.36]{d}{\delta} \dtwocell[-0.36]{d}{\beta} &
2036\U\text. \\
2037& & & &
2038}\]\vskip-0.5\baselineskip\noindent We must exhibit invertible
2039globular icon modifications
2040\[i_{(G, F)} \colon \id_{GF} \Rrightarrow \id_G \otimes \id_F \colon GF \Rightarrow GF \quad \text{and} \quad
2041m_{(\beta, \alpha), (\delta, \gamma)} \colon (\delta \otimes \gamma)(\beta
2042\otimes \alpha) \Rrightarrow (\delta \beta) \otimes (\gamma \alpha)\text;\] and
2043to do this, we take their respective $(A, B)$-components to be the invertible
2044modifications witnessing pseudo-functoriality of horizontal composition in the
2045following diagram of homomorphisms and pseudo-natural transformations:
2046\[\cd{
2047\S(A, B) \ar@/^2em/[rr]^{F_{A, B}} \ar[rr]|{F'_{A, B}} \ar@/_2em/[rr]_{F''_{A, B}} & {}\dtwocell[0.36]{d}{\gamma_{A, B}} \dtwocell[-0.36]{d}{\alpha_{A, B}} &
2048\T(FA, FB) \ar@/^2em/[rr]^{G_{FA, FB}} \ar[rr]|{G'_{FA, FB}} \ar@/_2em/[rr]_{G''_{FA, FB}} & {}\dtwocell[0.36]{d}{\delta_{FA, FB}} \dtwocell[-0.36]{d}{\beta_{FA, FB}} &
2049\sh{r}{0.75em} {\U(GFA, GFB)\text.} \\
2050& & & &
2051}\] We must check that these data satisfy axioms (MA1) and (MA2). The proof is straightforward
2052manipulation using the pseudo-naturality axioms for $\delta$ and the
2053modification axioms for $\Pi^\delta$. Finally, the naturality of the maps
2054$m_{(\beta, \alpha), (\delta, \gamma)}$ in all variables follows componentwise;
2055as do the coherence axioms which $m$ and $i$ must satisfy.
2056In order to complete the definition of $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$, all that remains is to give the
2057associativity and unitality constraints for top-level composition, and to check the triangle
2058and pentagon axioms.
2059At the level of 1-cells and vertical 2-cells, these are the corresponding constraints from $\cat{Tricat}_2$; whilst at the level of horizontal 2-cells and 3-cells, we suppose given trihomomorphisms and pseudo-icons \[\cd{ {\R} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{F} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{F'} \dtwocell{r}{\alpha} & {\S} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{G} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{G'} \dtwocell{r}{\beta} & {\T} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{H} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{H'} \dtwocell{r}{\gamma} & {\U\text,} }\] and must exhibit an invertible pseudo-icon modification \[ \cd[@+0.5em]{ (HG)F \ar@2[d]_{a_{F, G, H}} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{(\gamma \otimes \beta) \otimes \alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{a_{\alpha, \beta, \gamma}}& (H'G')F' \ar@2[d]^{a_{F', G', H'}} \\ H(GF) \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\gamma \otimes (\beta \otimes \alpha)} & H'(G'F') }\] where $a_{F, G, H}$ and $a_{F', G', H'}$ are the corresponding constraints from $\cat{Tricat}_2$.
2060So
2061we take the $(A, B)$th component of this pseudo-icon modification to be the cubical modification providing the associativity constraint for the composition \[\cd[@C+2.3em]{ {\R(A, B)} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{F_{A, B}} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{F'_{A, B}} \dtwocell[0.45]{r}{\alpha_{A, B}} & {\S(FA, FB)} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{G_{FA, FB}} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{G'_{FA, FB}} \dtwocell[0.37]{r}{\beta_{FA, FB}} & {\T(GFA, GFB)} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{H_{GFA, GFB}} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{H'_{GFA, GFB}} \dtwocell[0.32]{r}{\gamma_{GFA, GFB}} & {\U(HGFA, HGFB)} }\] in the locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Bicat}$.
2062We must check that
2063these data satisfy the axioms for an icon modification; let us do only (MA2),
2064since (MA1) is similar. We first observe that the 3-cells $\Pi^{(\gamma \otimes
2065\beta) \otimes \alpha}_A$ and $\Pi^{\gamma \otimes (\beta \otimes \alpha)}_A$
2066are obtained by pasting together what is essentially the same $3 \times 3$
2067diagram of 3-cells, and some trivial calculus with unnamed coherence cells
2068shows that they are precisely the same diagram, modulo rewriting of the
2069boundary, so that the latter 3-cell may be obtained from the former by pasting
2070with unnamed coherence cells. But this is precisely the content of axiom (MA2).
2071Finally, we must check that these icon modifications $a_{\alpha, \beta, \gamma}$ are natural
2072in in $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$, and satisfy the pentagon and triangle equalities. Each
2073of these follows componentwise from the corresponding facts in $\mathfrak{Bicat}$. This
2074completes the definition of $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$.
2075\section{From locally cubical bicategories to tricategories}\label{Sec:fromltt}
2076In the previous Section, we constructed a locally cubical bicategory of
2077tricategories which we called $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$. Recall from
2078Section~\ref{Sec:towards} that one reason for doing this was so that we could
2079deduce the existence of the tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$. The purpose of this
2080section is to describe the general machinery which will allow us to do this.
2081The construction takes a well-behaved locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak B$ and builds a
2082tricategory out of it. This tricategory will have the same 0-\ and 1-cells as $\mathfrak B$;
2083as 2-cells, the horizontal 2-cells of $\mathfrak B$; and as 3-cells, the globular 3-cells of
2084$\mathfrak B$. The main point of interest is the construction of the tricategorical
2085associativity constraints, which are to be given by \emph{horizontal} 2-cells of $\mathfrak
2086B$. Since the associativity constraints in $\mathfrak B$ are given by \emph{vertical} 2-cells,
2087we will need some kind of linkage between the two types of 2-cell in order to proceed.
2088\begin{Defn}
2089A pseudo double category $\mathfrak C$ is \defn{fibrant} if the functor $(s, t)
2090\colon \C_1 \to \C_0 \times \C_0$ is an isofibration.
2091\end{Defn}
2092\noindent Recall here that a functor $F \colon \A \to \B$ between categories is an \emph{isofibration} if whenever we have a object $a \in \A$ and isomorphism $\phi \colon Fa \to b$ in $\B$, there exists an object $c \in \A$ and isomorphism $\theta \colon a \to c$ such that $Fc = b$ and $F\theta = \phi$.
2093Thus
2094a pseudo double category $\mathfrak C$ is fibrant just when every diagram like (a) below with $f$ and $g$ isomorphisms has a filler like (b) for which the 2-cell $\theta$ is invertible as an arrow of $\C_1$: \[\text{(a)} \quad \cd{ x \ar[d]_{f} & x' \ar[d]^{g} \\ y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{k} & y'} \qquad \rightsquigarrow \qquad \text{(b)} \quad \cd{ x \ar[d]_{f} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{h} \dtwocell{dr}{\theta}& x' \ar[d]^{g} \\ y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{k} & y'\text.}\] Thus fibrancy is precisely the property which \cite{GP1} refers to as \emph{horizontal invariance}.
2095We may
2096reformulate this property in various useful ways, and since detailed accounts
2097of this process may be found in \cite{tomf} or \cite{GP2}, we restrict
2098ourselves here to recording those equivalent formulations which will be useful
2099to us.
2100For the first, we consider the case of the above filling condition where $g$
2101and $k$ are both identities: given a vertical map $f \colon x \to y$ of
2102$\mathfrak C$, it asserts the existence of a horizontal 1-cell $\overline f$
2103and a 2-cell $\epsilon_f$ fitting into the diagram:
2104\[\cd{
2105x \ar[d]_{f} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\overline f} \dtwocell{dr}{\epsilon_f}& y \ar[d]^{\id_y} \\
2106y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\DI y} & y\text.}\] From this, we may define a further 2-cell $\eta_f$ as
2107the composite
2108\[\cd{
2109x \ar[d]_{\id_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\DI x} \dtwocell{dr}{\eta_f} &
2110x \ar[d]^{f} \\
2111x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\overline f} & y} \quad := \quad \cd{
2112x \ar[d]_{f} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\DI x} \dtwocell{dr}{\DI f} &
2113x \ar[d]^{f} \\
2114y \ar[d]_{f^{-1}} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\overline f} \dtwocell{dr}{\epsilon_f^{-1}} &
2115y \ar[d]^{\id_y} \\
2116x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\overline f} & y\text.}\]
2117Now the pair $(\eta_f, \epsilon_f)$ satisfy the triangle identities:
2118\[\epsilon_f . \eta_f = \DI f \colon \DI x \Rightarrow \DI y \quad \text{and} \quad \epsilon_f \ast \eta_f = (l^{-1}r)_{\overline f} \colon \overline f . \DI x \Rightarrow \DI y . \overline f\text,\]
2119and so, in the terminology of \cite{GP2}, $f$ and $\overline f$ are
2120\emph{orthogonal companions}; which gives us the ``only if'' direction of:
2121\begin{Prop}
2122A pseudo double category $\mathfrak C$ is fibrant iff every vertical
2123isomorphism has an orthogonal companion.
2124\end{Prop}
2125\noindent For the ``if'' direction, suppose that we are given a diagram like
2126(a); then we can complete it to a diagram like (b) by taking $h$ to be
2127$\overline{g^{-1}} . (k . \overline f)$ and $\theta$ to be the 2-cell:
2128\[\overline{g^{-1}} . (k . \overline f) \xRightarrow{(\DI g .\epsilon_{g^{-1}}) \ast (\id_k \ast
2129\epsilon_f)} \DI{y'} . (k . \DI y) \xRightarrow{\DI{y'} \ast r_k} \DI{y'} .
2130k \xRightarrow{l_k} k\text.\]
2131Thus
2132each of $\mathfrak{Cat}$, $\mathfrak{Rng}$ and $\mathfrak{Span}(\C)$ is a fibrant double category: for $\mathfrak{Cat}$, the horizontal companion of a functor $F \colon \C \to D$ is the profunctor $\overline F(\mathord \thg, \mathord ?) = \D(\mathord \thg, F\mathord ?)$; for $\mathfrak{Rng}$, the companion of a homomorphism $f \colon R \to S$ is $S$ itself, viewed as a left $S$-, right $R$-module; and in $\mathfrak{Span}(\C)$, the companion of a morphism $f \colon C \to D$ is the span $C \stackrel{id}{\leftarrow} C \stackrel{f}{\rightarrow} D$.
2133Observe that in all of these examples, it is
2134arbitrary vertical morphisms, and not just the isomorphisms, which have
2135companions: such pseudo double categories are essentially the \emph{pro-arrow
2136equipments} of \cite{wood1, wood2}. A more detailed analysis of this
2137correspondence may be found in Appendix C of \cite{mike}.
2138\begin{Prop}
2139Let $\mathfrak C$ be a fibrant double category equipped with a choice of
2140orthogonal companion for every vertical isomorphism. Then the assignation $f
2141\mapsto \overline f$ underlies an identity-on-objects homomorphism of
2142bicategories
2143\[(\overline{\ \ \mathstrut})\colon V^{\text{iso}}(\mathfrak C) \to H(\mathfrak C)\text,\]
2144where $V^{\text{iso}}(\mathfrak C)$ is the category of objects and vertical
2145isomorphisms in $\mathfrak C$. Moreover, if we are given vertical isomorphisms
2146$f \colon w \to y$ and $g \colon x \to z$ in $\mathfrak C$, then pasting with
2147$\eta_f$ and $\epsilon_g$ induces a bijection between the set of 2-cells of the
2148form (c) and the set of 2-cells of the form (d):
2149\[(c) \quad \cd{
2150x \ar[d]_{f} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{h} \dtwocell{dr}{\alpha} & x' \ar[d]^{g} \\
2151y \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{k} & y'} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{(d)} \quad \cd{
2152x \ar[d]_{\id_x} \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\overline g . h} \dtwocell{dr}{\overline \alpha} & y' \ar[d]^{\id_{y'}} \\
2153x \ar[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{k . \overline f} & y'\text;}\] and $\overline \alpha$ is invertible
2154as an arrow of $\C_1$ just when $\alpha$ is. Furthermore, these bijections satisfy four
2155evident axioms expressing their functoriality with respect to vertical and horizontal
2156composition of 2-cells.\end{Prop}
2157If we remove the restriction to vertical isomorphisms,
2158then
2159the structure described in this Proposition is that of a \emph{pseudo folding structure} in the sense of \cite{tomf}.
2160The proof of the Proposition is straightforward manipulation, and it
2161is not hard to prove a converse~--~namely, that from a homomorphism of bicategories
2162$(\overline{\ \ \mathstrut})\colon V^{\text{iso}}(\mathfrak C) \to H(\mathfrak C)$ and a
2163bijective assignation $\alpha \mapsto \overline \alpha$ on 2-cells satisfying the four
2164functoriality axioms, one may define a choice of orthogonal companion for every vertical
2165isomorphism. A proof of this correspondence may be extracted from the pages leading up to
2166Theorem 3.28 of \cite{tomf}.
2167\begin{Defn}
2168The 2-category $\cat{DblCat}_f$ has objects being fibrant pseudo double
2169categories equipped with a choice of orthogonal companions; as 1-cells, the
2170homomorphisms between the underlying double categories; and as 2-cells, the
2171vertical transformations between them.
2172\end{Defn}
2173\noindent One may reasonably ask why we do not require the 1-cells $F \colon
2174\mathfrak C \to \mathfrak D$ of $\cat{DblCat}_f$ to respect the choices of
2175orthogonal companions in $\mathfrak C$ and $\mathfrak D$. The reason is that,
2176in fact, \emph{any} homomorphism between objects of $\cat{DblCat}_f$ will
2177automatically respect these choices in a unique way. To make this explicit, let
2178us say that a homomorphism $F \colon \mathfrak C \to \mathfrak D$ between
2179objects of $\cat{DblCat}_f$ is a
2180\defn{fibrant homomorphism} if, for every invertible vertical 1-cell $f \colon x \to y$ of $\mathfrak C$, there is given
2181an invertible globular 2-cell \[\mu_f \colon F(\overline f) \Rightarrow
2182\overline{Ff} \colon Fx \tor Fy\] of $\mathfrak D$, subject to three axioms.
2183The first two equate, respectively, the two possible 2-cells in $\mathfrak D$
2184from $\DI {Fx}$ to $\overline{F(\id_x)}$; and from $F(\overline g) \, . \, F
2185(\overline f)$ to $\overline{F(gf)}$. The third axiom concerns a 2-cell
2186$\alpha$ of the type (c) above, and equates the two globular 2-cells
2187\[
2188\cd[@-1em]{
2189Fx \ar@/_4em/[dd]|-{\object@{|}}_{\overline {Ff}} \ar[dd]|-{\object@{|}}_{F(\overline f)} \ar[rr]|-{\object@{|}}^{Fh} \dtwocell{ddrr}{F(\overline \alpha)} && x' \ar[dd]|-{\object@{|}}^{F(\overline g)} \\
2190{}\ltwocell[-0.9]{r}{\mu_f} &
2191\\
2192Fy \ar[rr]|-{\object@{|}}_{Fk} && Fy'} \quad \text{and} \quad \cd[@-1em]{
2193Fx \ar[dd]|-{\object@{|}}_{\overline {Ff}} \ar[rr]|-{\object@{|}}^{Fh} \dtwocell{ddrr}{\overline {F\alpha}} && x' \ar[dd]|-{\object@{|}}^{\overline {Fg}} \ar@/^4em/[dd]|-{\object@{|}}^{F(\overline g)} \\
2194& & {}\ltwocell[-0.9]{l}{\mu_f}
2195\\
2196Fy \ar[rr]|-{\object@{|}}_{Fk} && Fy'\text.}
2197\]
2198Now, given any homomorphism $F \colon \mathfrak C \to \mathfrak D$ between
2199objects of $\cat{DblCat}_f$, we may make it into a fibrant homomorphism as
2200follows. Given an invertible vertical arrow $f \colon x \to y$ of $\mathfrak
2201C$, we can consider the globular 2-cell
2202\[\overline{F\epsilon_f} \colon \overline{\id_{Fy}} . F (\overline f)
2203\Rightarrow F\DI y . \overline{Ff}\] of $\mathfrak D$; and since both $\overline{\id_{Fy}}$
2204and $F\DI y$ are isomorphic to $\DI {Fy}$, we obtain from this a globular 2-cell $\mu_f \colon
2205F (\overline f) \Rightarrow \overline{Ff}$, which is easily checked to satisfy the three
2206axioms. And in fact, this is the only possible structure of fibrant homomorphism on $F$: for
2207given an arbitrary such structure, applying the third axiom to the 2-cells $\epsilon_f$ in
2208$\mathfrak C$ shows that the maps $\mu_f$ must coincide with those defined above. A
2209similar argument applies to the 2-cells of $\cat{DblCat}_f$.
2210A conceptual explanation of why this should be the case is that
2211$\cat{DblCat}_f$ is, in some sense, the 2-category of algebras for a
2212particularly simple kind of 2-dimensional monad on $\cat{DblCat}$, the kind
2213which \cite{propertylike} calls \emph{pseudo-idempotent}: and such monads have
2214the property that the forgetful functor from the 2-category of algebras and
2215algebra pseudomorphisms to the underlying base 2-category is 2-fully faithful.
2216The qualifier ``in some sense'' covers a slight wrinkle in this explanation:
2217namely, that the 2-monad which gives rise to $\cat{DblCat}_f$ lives not on
2218$\cat{DblCat}$ but on $\cat{DblCat}_\text{str}$, the 2-category of pseudo
2219double categories and \emph{strict} homomorphisms between them, so that making
2220this argument rigourous would require a little more work.
2221\begin{Defn}
2222We will say that a locally cubical bicategory is \defn{locally fibrant} just
2223when each of its hom-double categories is fibrant.
2224\end{Defn}
2225In particular, a monoidal double category is locally fibrant just when its
2226underlying pseudo double category is fibrant, so that all of our examples of
2227monoidal double categories are locally fibrant. The locally cubical bicategory
2228$\mathfrak{DblCat}$ is easily seen \emph{not} to be locally fibrant; on the
2229other hand, we may show that, for pseudo double categories $\mathfrak C$ and
2230$\mathfrak D$, if $\mathfrak D$ is fibrant then so is $\HOM{\mathfrak C,
2231\mathfrak D}$. It follows that the locally cubical bicategory
2232$\mathfrak{DblCat}_f$, of fibrant double categories and all cells between them,
2233is itself locally fibrant; and since any bicategory is trivially fibrant, that
2234the locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Bicat}$ is too.
2235We will now show that every locally fibrant locally cubical bicategory gives
2236rise to a tricategory. We begin with a technical result:
2237\begin{Prop}\label{trihomom}
2238Let $\cat{DblCat}_g$ be the maximal sub-2-category of $\cat{DblCat}_f$ with
2239only invertible 2-cells. Then the functor of mere categories $\cat{DblCat}_g
2240\hookrightarrow \cat{DblCat} \xrightarrow \HH \cat{Bicat}$ can be extended to a
2241trihomomorphism
2242\[\HH \colon \cat{DblCat}_g \to \cat{Bicat}\text.\]
2243\end{Prop}
2244\begin{proof}
2245First we define $\HH$ on cells.
2246This is already done for 0-\ and 1-cells, and
2247since $\cat{DblCat}_g$ has no non-trivial 3-cells, it remains only to define it on 2-cells.
2248So
2249let there be given an invertible vertical transformation $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G \colon \mathfrak C \to \mathfrak D$.
2250We define a
2251pseudo-natural transformation $\HH\alpha \colon \HH F \Rightarrow \HH G$ by
2252taking
2253\[(\HH \alpha)_x = \overline{\alpha_x} \colon Fx \to Gx\text, \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\HH \alpha)_f = \cd{
2254Fx \ar[d]_{\overline{\alpha_x}} \ar[r]^{Ff} \dtwocell{dr}{\overline{\alpha_f}}& Fy \ar[d]^{\overline{\alpha_y}} \\
2255Gx \ar[r]_{Gf} & Gy\text.}\] The transformation axioms for $\HH\alpha$ follow straightforwardly
2256from the vertical transformation axioms for $\alpha$ and the functoriality of
2257$(\overline{\ \ \mathstrut})$ with respect to 2-cell composition. Next we
2258ensure that $\HH$ is locally a homomorphism of bicategories, which entails
2259giving modifications $i_F \colon \id_{\HH F} \Rrightarrow \HH(\id_F)$ and
2260$m_{\alpha, \beta} \colon
2261\HH \beta . \HH \alpha\Rrightarrow \HH(\beta . \alpha)$. These will have 2-cell components
2262\[(i_F)_x \colon \id_{Fx} \Rightarrow \overline{\id_{Fx}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (m_{\alpha, \beta})_x \colon \overline{\beta_x} \, . \, \overline{\alpha_x} \Rightarrow \overline{\beta_x \alpha_x}\]
2263in $\HH \mathfrak D$ given by the pseudo-functoriality constraints for
2264$(\overline{\ \ \mathstrut})$. The coherence axioms for these data therefore
2265follow pointwise.
2266Next, we must give adjoint pseudo-natural equivalences \[{\b \chi}_{\mathfrak C, \mathfrak D, \mathfrak E} \colon \HH(\thg) \otimes \HH(?) \Rightarrow \HH(\thg \otimes ?) \colon \cat{DblCat}_g(\mathfrak C, \mathfrak D) \times \cat{DblCat}_g(\mathfrak B, \mathfrak C) \to \cat{Bicat}(\HH \mathfrak B, \HH \mathfrak D)\text.\] Observe that the homomorphisms $\HH(\thg) \otimes \HH(?)$ and $\HH(\mathord \thg \otimes \mathord ?)$ agree on objects, and thus we may consider icons between them: in particular, any \emph{invertible} icon between them will give rise to an adjoint pseudo-natural equivalence, and so to give $\chi$ it suffices to give invertible icons $\chi \colon \HH(\thg) \otimes \HH(?) \Rightarrow \HH(\mathord \thg \otimes \mathord ?)$.
2267So
2268consider a pair of horizontally composable 2-cells
2269\[\cd{ {\mathfrak B} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{F} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{F'} \dtwocell{r}{\alpha} & {\mathfrak C} \ar@/^1em/[r]^{G} \ar@/_1em/[r]_{G'} \dtwocell{r}{\beta} & {\mathfrak D} }\]in $\cat{DblCat}_g$: we must give a modification $\chi_{\alpha, \beta} \colon \HH \beta \ast \HH
2270\alpha \Rrightarrow \HH(\beta \ast \alpha)$.
2271Now, these two pseudo-natural
2272transformations have respective $x$-components given by \begin{align*} (\HH
2273\beta \ast \HH \alpha)_x & = GFx \xrightarrow{\overline{\beta_{Fx}}} G'Fx
2274\xrightarrow{G'\overline{\alpha_x}} G'F'x\\ \text{and\ \ } \HH(\beta \ast
2275\alpha)_x & = GFx \xrightarrow{\overline{G'{\alpha_x} . \beta_{Fx}}}
2276G'F'x\text,\end{align*} and so we take $(\chi_{\alpha, \beta})_x$ to be the
22772-cell
2278\[G'\overline{\alpha_x} \, . \, \overline{\beta_{Fx}} \xRightarrow{\mu_{\alpha_x} . 1} \overline{G'\alpha_x} \, . \, \overline{\beta_{Fx}} \xRightarrow{\ \cong\ } \overline{G'\alpha_x . \beta_{Fx}}\]
2279of $\HH \mathfrak D$. The modification axioms for $\chi_{\alpha, \beta}$ follow
2280from the third fibrant homomorphism axiom and the functoriality axioms for
2281$(\overline{\ \ \mathstrut})$ with respect to 2-cell composition. We must
2282verify that these components $\chi_{\alpha, \beta}$ satisfy the three axioms
2283making $\chi$ into an icon. The first is vacuous, whilst the second and third
2284follow by a diagram chase using the axioms for a fibrant homomorphism. We argue
2285entirely analogously in order to give the adjoint equivalences $\iota \colon
2286I_{\HH x} \Rightarrow \HH(I_x)$.
2287Next we must give invertible modifications $\omega$, $\delta$ and $\gamma$. In
2288the case of $\omega$, for instance, this involves giving invertible
2289modifications
2290\[\cd[@!C@!R@R+1em]{
2291& (\HH(\thg)\otimes\HH(?))\otimes\HH(\mathord \ast)
2292\ar@2[dl]_{\chi \otimes 1} \ar@2[dr]^{\a} \\
2293\HH(\mathord \thg \otimes \mathord ?)\otimes\HH(\mathord\ast)
2294\ar@2[d]_{\chi} \rthreecell{drr}{\omega} & &
2295\HH(\thg) \otimes (\HH(?) \otimes \HH(\mathord \ast))
2296\ar@2[d]^{1 \otimes \chi} \\
2297\HH((\mathord \thg \otimes \mathord ?) \otimes \mathord \ast)
2298\ar@2[dr]_{\HH\a} & &
2299\HH(\thg) \otimes \HH(\mathord ? \otimes \mathord \ast)
2300\ar@2[dl]^{\chi} \\ &
2301\HH(\thg \otimes (\mathord ? \otimes \mathord \ast))\text.
2302}\] To do this, observe first that every pseudo-natural transformation bounding this diagram may
2303also be viewed as an icon. We already know this for $\chi$ and hence also for
2304$1 \otimes \chi$ and $\chi \otimes 1$; and it is so for $\a$ and $\HH \a$ since
2305composition of 1-cells in both $\cat{DblCat}_g$ and $\cat{Bicat}$ is
2306\emph{strictly} associative. If we now compose all the 2-arrows in this diagram
2307\emph{qua} icons, we obtain two further icons $\sigma, \tau \colon
2308(\HH(\thg)\otimes\HH(?))\otimes\HH(\mathord \ast) \Rightarrow \HH(\thg \otimes
2309(\mathord ? \otimes \mathord \ast))$: and a long but straightforward diagram
2310chase with the fibrant homomorphism axioms shows that these two icons are, in
2311fact, equal.
2312On the other hand, if we compose the two sides \emph{qua} pseudo-natural transformations, then the pseudo-naturals that we get will not necessarily be icons, but they will, at least, be \emph{isomorphic} to icons, namely the icons $\sigma$ and $\tau$ respectively.
2313Thus
2314we take $\omega$ to be the composite of the invertible modification from the left-hand side of this diagram to $\sigma = \tau$ and the invertible modification from $\tau$ to the right-hand side.
2315We
2316proceed similarly for the invertible modifications $\delta$ and $\gamma$.
2317The final thing to check are the two trihomomorphism axioms, equating certain
2318pastings of 3-cells in $\cat{Bicat}$. But all the 3-cells in question are
2319either coherence 3-cells of $\cat{Bicat}$; or component 3-cells of $\omega$,
2320$\delta$ and $\gamma$. But these latter 3-cells are in turn built from
2321coherence 3-cells of $\cat{Bicat}$ and coherence 3-cells for the local
2322homomorphisms $(\overline{\ \ \mathstrut})$. The result thus follows by
2323coherence for tricategories and bicategorical coherence for functors.
2324\end{proof}
2325\begin{Thm}\label{locallydoubletotri}
2326Let $\mathfrak C$ be a locally fibrant locally cubical bicategory with chosen
2327companions in each hom. Then there is a tricategory $\T$ with the same objects
2328as $\mathfrak C$, and
2329\[\T(A, B) = \HH\big(\mathfrak C(A, B)\big)\text.\]
2330\end{Thm}
2331\begin{proof}
2332We begin by observing that both $\cat{DblCat}_g$ and $\cat{Bicat}$ come
2333equipped with finite product structure; and that the trihomomorphism $\HH$
2334preserves the cartesian product of $j$-cells for $j = 0, 1, 2, 3$. Now, the
2335top-level composition and identity functors for $\T$ are given by applying
2336$\HH$ to the corresponding data (LDD3) and (LDD4) for $\mathfrak C$:
2337\[1 = \HH 1 \xrightarrow{\HH \elt{I_A}} \HH\big(\mathfrak C(A, A)) = \T(A, A)\]
2338and
2339\[\T(B, C) \times \T(A, B) = \HH\big(\mathfrak C(B, C) \times \mathfrak C(A, B)\big) \xrightarrow{\HH \mathord \otimes} \HH\big(\mathfrak C(A, C)\big) = \T(A, C)\text.\]
2340To obtain the pseudo-natural adjoint equivalences $\a$, $\l$ and $\r$
2341witnessing the associativity and unitality of this composition, we apply $\HH$
2342to the corresponding data (LDD5) and (LDD6) for $\mathfrak C$. Since each of
2343$a$, $l$ and $r$ is an adjoint equivalence (in fact, an isomorphism) in the
2344relevant hom of $\cat{DblCat}_g$, the same will obtain for their images in
2345$\cat{Bicat}$; and because $\HH$ strictly preserves both cartesian products and
2346composition of 1-cells, these adjoint equivalences will have the correct
2347sources and targets.
2348Next we must give the invertible modifications $\pi$, $\mu$, $\lambda$ and
2349$\rho$. To obtain $\pi$, for example, we begin by applying $\HH$ to the axiom
2350(LDA2) for $\mathfrak C$. This yields an equality of 2-cells in $\cat{Bicat}$;
2351however, these 2-cells are not of the right form to be the source and target of
2352$\pi$.
2353In order to make them so, we may adjust by coherence 3-cells in $\cat{Bicat}$ whose existence is guaranteed by the coherence theorem for trihomomorphisms.
2354Consequently,
2355we may take $\pi$ to be given by the composite of these coherence 3-cells; and similarly for $\mu$, $\lambda$ and $\rho$.
2356Finally, we must check the three tricategory axioms. These are normally stated
2357in a ``local'' form, asserting the equality of certain pastings of 3-cells in
2358the relevant hom-bicategories; but in this situation, it will be more
2359appropriate to consider them in their ``global'' form. Each such axiom amounts
2360to giving a diagram of 2-\ and 3-cells in $\cat{Bicat}$, whose vertices are
2361pasting diagrams built from copies of the 2-cells $a$, $l$ and $r$, and whose
2362arrows are 3-cells between those 2-cells, built from copies of $\pi$, $\mu$,
2363$\lambda$ and $\rho$; and asserting that the two ways around this diagram
2364coincide.
2365To show this, we consider the corresponding diagram for $\mathfrak C$.
2366This is a diagram of 2-\ and 3-cells in $\cat{DblCat_g}$, which since $\cat{DblCat}_g$ has only identity 3-cells, must commute.
2367Hence
2368by applying $\HH$ we obtain a commutative diagram in $\cat{Bicat}$, which, unfortunately, has both the wrong vertices and the wrong arrows.
2369Nonetheless, by the coherence theorem for
2370functors, each ``wrong'' vertex admits an isomorphism 3-cell to the ``right''
2371vertex; and in such a way that composing these isomorphism 3-cells with the
2372``wrong'' arrows yields the ``right'' arrows.
2373\end{proof}
2374Special cases of this theorem give us new proofs of some existing results.
2375Restricting to the one-object case, we have the result that \emph{any fibrant
2376monoidal double category gives rise to a monoidal bicategory}; this statement
2377and a sketch proof appear as Theorem B.4 of \cite{mike}. In particular, we
2378obtain elegant proofs that the bicategories of rings and bimodules, of
2379categories and profunctors, and of spans internal to a cartesian category $\C$
2380are all monoidal bicategories.\footnote{For the last two of these examples, the
2381machinery of \cite{cb2} provides another elegant proof of this fact, and in
2382fact goes further, showing that the monoidal bicategories in question are
2383\emph{symmetric} monoidal bicategories.}\ \ Finally, applying this theorem to
2384the fibrant locally cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Bicat}$, we deduce the
2385existence of a tricategory of bicategories $\cat{Bicat}$. Again, the result is
2386not new, but the proof is, showing how the tricategory structure on
2387$\cat{Bicat}$ may be induced from a piece of canonical, universally determined
2388structure, namely the biclosed structure on $\cat{DblCat}$.
2389\section{A tricategory of tricategories}\label{tritri}
2390We are now finally in a position to prove Theorem \ref{mainresultprop}, which
2391asserts the existence of the tricategory of tricategories $\cat{Tricat}_3$. We
2392will do this by applying the machinery of the previous section to the locally
2393cubical bicategory $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$. In order to do this, we must first
2394prove that $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3$ is locally fibrant.
2395\begin{Prop}
2396Each pseudo double category $\mathfrak{Tricat}_3(\S, \T)$ is fibrant.
2397\end{Prop}
2398\begin{proof}
2399Suppose we are given an invertible ico-icon $\alpha \colon F \Rightarrow G
2400\colon \S \to \T$. We must provide a pseudo-icon $\overline \alpha \colon F
2401\Tor G$ and an invertible icon modification
2402\[\cd{
2403F \ar@2[d]_{\alpha} \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}^{\overline \alpha} \dthreecell{dr}{\epsilon_\alpha}& G \ar@2[d]^{\id_G} \\
2404G \ar@2[r]|-{\object@{|}}_{\DI G} & G.
2405}\] Now by Proposition \ref{embed}, there is a bijection between the ico-icons $F \Rightarrow G$ and the oplax icons $F \Tor G$ with identity 2-cell components: for which the invertible ico-icons on the one side correspond to the pseudo-icons on the other.
2406Thus
2407we take $\overline \alpha$ to be the pseudo-icon corresponding to $\alpha$ under this bijection.
2408To give the icon modification $\epsilon_\alpha$, we must give 3-cells
2409$(\epsilon_\alpha)_f \colon {\overline \alpha}_f \Rrightarrow (\DI G)_f$ of
2410$\T$, forming the components of an $\ob \S \times \ob \S$-indexed family of
2411cubical modifications, and satisfying axioms (MA1) and (MA2). Since we have
2412${\overline \alpha}_f = (\DI G)_f = \id_{Ff} \colon Ff \Rightarrow Ff$, we take
2413$(\epsilon_\alpha)_f = \id_{\id_f}$. The cubical modification axioms and axioms
2414(MA1) and (MA2) now follow by coherence for bicategories.
2415\end{proof}
2416And so finally we obtain:
2417\begin{Cor}\label{finalresult}
2418There is a tricategory $\cat{Tricat}_3$ with objects being tricategories;
24191-cells, lax homomorphisms; 2-cells, pseudo-icons; and 3-cells, pseudo-icon
2420modifications.
2421\end{Cor}
2422\begin{Cor}
2423The tricategory $\cat{MonBicat}$ of monoidal bicategories, weak monoidal
2424functors, weak monoidal transformations, and monoidal modifications is
2425triequivalent to the full sub-tricategory of $\cat{Tricat}_{3}$ consisting of
2426those tricategories with a single object.
2427\end{Cor}
